Home Awards Winner Announcements PRESS RELEASE: Global Finance Names The 100 Safest Banks In The World For 2026
Global Finance has announced its 35th annual ranking of the World’s Safest Banks for 2026.
The full list of the 100 Safest Banks in the World is included here and will be published in the November print and digital editions, and at GFMag.com.
European banks dominate Global Finance’s rankings once again in 2026, taking the top 12 positions, 17 of the top 25, and more than half of the top 50. Germany’s KfW is #1 for the 17th year in a row.
A total of 28 countries, territories, and districts made the top 100 for 2026. France landed the most with 10 ranked banks, followed by Germany, South Korea, and the United States with eight, and Canada with seven.
“In a period of continued economic uncertainty, geopolitical tension and rapid change across the financial sector, strength, stability and disciplined risk management remain critical measures of banking excellence. Global Finance’s World’s Safest Banks 2026 recognizes the institutions that have demonstrated the financial strength and long-term resilience needed to navigate emerging risks and provide confidence to customers and markets,” said Joseph Giarraputo, founder and editorial director of Global Finance.
Global Finance’s annual rankings of the World’s Safest Banks have been the recognized and trusted standard of financial counterparty safety for more than three decades. Winners were selected through an evaluation of long-term foreign currency ratings of the 500 largest banks worldwide from Moody’s, Standard & Poor’s, and Fitch.
In addition to the 100 Safest Banks in the World, the full report also includes the following: World’s 50 Safest Commercial Banks; Safest Banks by Country, Territory, and District; 50 Safest Banks in Emerging Markets; Safest Islamic Financial Institutions in the GCC; and Safest Banks by Region (Africa, Asia, Australasia, Central & Eastern Europe, Latin America, the Middle East, North America, and Western Europe).
For editorial information please contact: Denise Bedell – dbedell@gfmag.com
Ratings current as of: August 27, 2026 / Press Release Date: October 6, 2026
Global Finance, founded in 1987, has a circulation of 50,000 readers in 196 countries, territories, and districts. Global Finance’s audience includes senior corporate and financial officers responsible for making investment and strategic decisions at multinational companies and financial institutions. Its website — GFMag.com — offers analysis and articles that are the legacy of 39 years of experience in international financial markets. Global Finance is headquartered in New York, with offices around the world. Global Finance regularly selects the top performers among banks and other providers of financial services. These awards have become a trusted standard of excellence for the global financial community.

articles.title_orig: EU trade Commissioner to speak with China over growing deficit
articles.title_zh: EU trade Commissioner to speak with China over growing deficit
articles.content_orig:
By ELIANA SILVER, SENIOR FOREIGN NEWS REPORTER
Published: 06:17 EDT, 8 October 2026 | Updated: 06:22 EDT, 8 October 2026
The EU and China are edging closer to a trade war, with the bloc’s commerce chief warning that its trade deficit with China is ‘unsustainable’ as he began two days of talks in Beijing aimed at averting an escalating confrontation.
Beijing, meanwhile, hit back by warning that Europe lacks the capacity to wage a trade war, issuing a blunt challenge: ‘Let them try.’
Writing on X on Thursday, European Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security Maros Sefcovic said: 'Day one in China, with one goal: begin rebalancing our... unsustainable trade deficit.'
'I started by hearing directly from EU businesses here. The message around the table was clear: the need to improve access to the Chinese market, while boosting our economic security,' he added.
Last year, every day, China exported to the EU around a billion euros more in goods and services than went the other way, according to European figures.
Many in Europe blame this on unfair trade practices by Beijing, including state subsidies and price dumping, undercutting European rivals in industries from cars to chemicals.
The Asian giant could throttle supplies of items such as rare earth minerals that are vital for the continent's industrial sector – or throw up barriers to European exports to China.
The two days of discussions by Mr Sefcovic in Beijing come as France and Germany, the bloc's two biggest powers, threaten to up the ante.
Last year, every day, China exported to the EU around a billion euros more in goods and services than went the other way, according to European figures (pictured: Xi Jinping)
In a letter earlier this week, President Emmanuel Macron and Chancellor Friedrich Merz called for a 'credible instrument' to respond quickly to any escalation by Beijing
In a letter earlier this week, President Emmanuel Macron and Chancellor Friedrich Merz called for a 'credible instrument' to respond quickly to any escalation by Beijing.
The proposed weapon – to be discussed at an EU leaders' summit next week – would give the European Commission the power to respond to a trade aggression within days.
Among other actions, it proposed making it easier for the European Commission to use the bloc's so-called 'trade bazooka', the Anti-Coercion Instrument.
This is a never-used-before raft of measures for blocking or restricting trade and investment from countries found to be putting undue pressure on EU member nations or corporations.
Yet not all EU nations agree on such tough measures. Spain, the eurozone's fourth-largest economy, has been less adversarial toward China in recent years.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has visited Beijing four times in three years. Far-Right and Left-wing lawmakers from Ireland to Bulgaria formed an unusual coalition on Wednesday to vote against resolution calling for tougher China policies.
China immediately warned Paris and Berlin on Tuesday against 'protectionist' measures.
'They should avoid going down the wrong path in the wrong way, only to ultimately suffer the consequences themselves,' the commerce ministry said in a statement.
And an editorial in China's state run Global Times newspaper read: 'The EU does not have the capacity to wage a trade war against China. If it is truly determined to do so, then let it try.'
China's foreign ministry said Thursday that Beijing hopes that it can work with Brussels 'in the same direction and address each other's concerns through dialogue and consultation'.
'As a principle, China has always believed that adhering to openness and cooperation and resolving economic and trade differences through equal dialogue and consultation is in the common interests of both China and the EU,' spokesman Mao Ning told a regular briefing.
The stakes are also high for President Xi Jinping, however, with China heavily reliant on exports in order to compensate for its stuttering domestic economy.
The EU parliament's trade committee chief, Bernd Lange, said ahead of Mr Sefcovic's trip that this 'economic crisis in China' gives the bloc 'bargaining power'.
'The EU has a well-supplied toolbox to counter unfair subsidies, dumping, discriminatory procurement, and economic coercion. These instruments must be applied consistently and, where necessary, enhanced,' Mr Lange said in a statement.
EU and Chinese officials have been negotiating since June, and Mr Sefcovic raised hopes earlier this year when he said that he wanted 'tangible results by October'.
Mr Sefcovic has identified three priorities: addressing surging imports in strategically important sectors, increasing European exports to China and improving access to critical raw materials.
The EU is also seeking clearer export-licensing arrangements for rare earths and other materials after China introduced restrictions last year.
Brussels hopes to manage Chinese exports through voluntary limits, for example on hybrid cars shipped to the bloc. Beijing, though, firmly opposes import quotas.
Analysts are cautious about the prospects for a broad agreement being struck this week.
Maros Sefcovic said: 'Day one in China, with one goal: begin rebalancing our... unsustainable trade deficit'
The EU imports sizable amounts of Chinese lithium-ion batteries and hybrid electric vehicles (Pictured: Workers produce transmissions for new energy vehicles in Wuhu)
Workers use machinery to dig at a rare earth mine in Ganxian county in central China's Jiangxi province
'But if one sector could be identified in which an export-restraint agreement with China could be tested, that would be a good step,' Ignacio Garcia Bercero, from Brussels think-tank Bruegel, said.
Zhu Tian, economics professor at Shanghai's China Europe International Business School, agreed, saying that the talks could yield agreements 'on some specific issues'.
Politicians and economists across the 27-nation bloc consider China's massive subsidies and exports a major threat to core industrial sectors from steel foundries to car factories.
China diverted many of its exports to the EU and other markets after the US raised tariffs.
In a debate Tuesday in European Parliament in Strasbourg, lawmakers overwhelmingly expressed anxiety alongside defiance over trade with China.
On Wednesday, they voted 454 to 86 on a resolution to toughen up on China that centered on a call for 'economic reciprocity and a proportionate EU response if China does not open its markets'.
Ahead of the vote, Hilde Vautmans, the Belgian lawmaker who led the resolution, said that 'Europe has economic power, it's time we used it.'
Despite the seeming European unity this week, it remains unclear what the EU can or is willing to do. It has already rolled out trade measures against Chinese steel imports and e-commerce small parcels.
France's High Commission for Strategy and Planning in February called for swift action, like 30 per cent tariffs on many of China's exports, and a devaluation of the euro against the Chinese currency.
Sales of German autos are plummeting in China but China is also poised to gobble up market share in Europe by undercutting European automakers on price thanks to heavy state subsidies.
There have already been mass layoffs at major manufacturers like Volkswagen.
The European Policy Centre in Brussels said in June that European battery producers, solar panels, steel, electric vehicles, chemicals and machinery are already haemorrhaging jobs and capacity and called for a trade investigative body modelled on Section 301 of the US Trade Act.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the phenomenon another 'China shock' for Europe, similar to what happened in the U.S. in the early 2000s when hundreds of thousands of factory jobs in the American heartland were wiped out.
The EU's ailing economy requires both a domestic overhaul and a more aggressive foreign trade policy, especially with China, said Tim Rühlig, a China analyst at the European Union I

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Oil Rises, Nasdaq Slips After Fresh Tanker Attack — Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Oil Rises, Nasdaq Slips After Fresh Tanker Attack — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices rose sharply Thursday, as Iran ramped up its attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz and Hurricane Isaias threatened U.S. offshore production in the Gulf of Mexico.
Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, gained 3.8% to $104.04 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures advanced 3.4% at $91.28.
Nine tankers have come under attack in and around Hormuz over the past week, jeopardizing the recent recovery in crude oil flows through the strait
Oil prices backed off session highs after President Donald Trump said the U.S. would not attack Iran before the November midterm elections. NBC News, citing unnamed sources, reported earlier that Trump and his national security team were considering renewing strikes in the coming weeks.
Some 9.5 million barrels per day exited Hormuz during the week ended Tuesday, about 30% below normal levels before the Iran war, according to Kpler data. Crude flows from the Middle East, including pipeline workarounds, stood at 16.4 million bpd which is nearly equivalent to prewar levels.
In the Gulf of Mexico, oil companies have shut in about 500,000 bpd, or 25% of offshore production in the region, as Hurricane Isaias churns toward the coasts of Alabama, Mississippi and the Florida panhandle.
Tensions are sharply escalating in the Middle East. Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen fired missiles at airports in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh and the city of Abha on Tuesday and Wednesday. Three people died and 36 were injured, according to the state-owned media outlet Al Arabiya.
The Saudis intercepted another volley of ballistic missiles fired Thursday at Riyadh and Khamis Mushait, a spokesperson for the kingdom's military said.
"While flows from the region have largely normalized, the need for US navy escorts, increased costs and logistical frictions and constant risk of being attacked call into question the longer-term feasibility of the flows," said Ryan McKay, director of commodity strategy at TD Securities.
"This ultimately warrants a sticky risk premium to remain in pricing," McKay told clients in a Thursday note.

articles.title_orig: Russian attack on buses in Ukraine’s Kramatorsk kills at least 30 people
articles.title_zh: Russian attack on buses in Ukraine’s Kramatorsk kills at least 30 people
articles.content_orig:
Zelenskyy says Kremlin deliberately targeted ‘ordinary public transport stop’ in Kramatorsk, with 18 wounded
A Russian missile strike on a bus in the eastern city of Kramatorsk has killed at least 30 people, officials have said, in one of the worst attacks by Moscow on Ukrainian civilians this year.
The regional prosecutor’s office in the Donetsk region said on Thursday the vehicle had been hit at 10am by an aerial bomb. “As of now, the death toll from this morning’s attack has risen to 30. Eighteen people were wounded,” it said, adding that all local public transport had been suspended.
Images ​posted by police ‌showed bodies ‌strewn across a street littered with debris, as well ‌as a charred shell of what appeared to be a bus. A second bus had also caught fire, officials said. The strike targeted an area next to a dental clinic on the city’s Yuvileina Street.
Three people had also been killed by shelling in the village of Bilenke, outside Kramatorsk, they added. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the Kremlin had deliberately targeted an “ordinary public transport stop”.
Some of those killed could not be identified because of the severity of their injuries, Ukraine’s president added. He said the number of victims could “sadly rise”, as doctors fought to save the lives of those wounded.
He said: “This strike will not go unanswered. Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and a response from the world is a must. A forceful response – exactly as the Russians deserve for all the deaths they have brought. May all those killed rest in peace.”
The bombing follows a gruesome Russian strike on Wednesday on a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky in the northern Chernihiv region. The building collapsed, entombing those inside. At least 22 people were killed, including five children, aged between one and eight.
Visiting the scene with Ed Miliband, the British foreign secretary, Zelenskyy urged the US to expand Starlink satellite internet coverage so that Ukraine could hit targets inside Russia such as launch sites. So far, Donald Trump and Elon Musk have refused Kyiv’s request.
Miliband said there was “no clearer sign of Putin’s evil, evil intent and strategy in this conflict” than this week’s murderous attacks. He said: “Putin once said that he was going to win on the battlefield. He is trying to win by terrorising civilians.”
Writing earlier on social media, Zelenskyy called on western allies to take “concrete steps” to boost Ukraine’s depleted air defences, amid a round-the-clock Russian onslaught in recent weeks featuring ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones.
“Supplies of anti-ballistic capabilities, ammunition for our combat aircraft, and investments in interceptors – all of this is directly helping save lives every day. Important talks with our partners will take place today and tomorrow,” Zelenskyy said.
Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk form part of a “fortress belt” . They are the last two big cities in northern Donetsk under full Ukrainian military control. Russia has been trying to capture them for more than a decade, after a brief period in which Russian forces occupied Sloviansk in 2014.
after newsletter promotion
The cities are home to thousands of civilians, as well as Ukrainian soldiers. In recent months, roads have been festooned with nets to protect traffic from marauding enemy drones. These defences offer little protection, however, against aerial bombs.
“These are not ‘the consequences of war’, nor dry statistics. These are people killed by the Russian army,” the Donetsk regional governor, Vadym Filashkin, said ‌on Telegram after Thursday’s strike. “Russia comes to Ukrainian land with death.”
He added: “The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians. For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible.
“Russia deliberately flouts every conceivable rule of warfare and the norms of international humanitarian law. It selects targets where it can inflict the greatest suffering on civilians.”
There was criticism of the White House’s policy of engaging with Vladimir Putin, whom Donald Trump has invited to December’s G20 summit in Miami, Florida. The Kremlin has yet to say if Russia’s leader will take part.
The former US ambassador to Moscow Michael McFaul said on social media that Russia was guilty of terrorism. “There is no other word for it. Putin is running a terrorist state. That officials from my country call this terrorist a nice guy is deeply embarrassing for me.”
Putin has demanded Ukraine cede the rest ​of ​the eastern Donbas region still under its ​control. Kyiv refuses to hand over its territory, believing Russia will take any concessions and carry on fighting.

articles.title_orig: Andreeva beats Alexandrova to reach China Open semifinals and next faces Bartunkova
articles.title_zh: Andreeva beats Alexandrova to reach China Open semifinals and next faces Bartunkova
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING (AP) — French Open champion Mirra Andreeva reached the semifinals of the China Open after battling past Ekaterina Alexandrova 7-6 (4), 7-6 (3) on Thursday.
Andreeva had lost her previous two matches against Alexandrova, who rallied back from 4-1 down in the second set and 5-3 down with Andreeva serving for the match.
“I felt like she was playing better and I didn’t take my chances. I could have played more aggressive but what a match this was,” Andreeva said. “She played unbelievable today, and I’m very happy to get my very first win against her.”
The fourth-seeded Andreeva is aiming for a fourth singles title this year and next faces Nikola Bartunkova. She earlier reached her first WTA 1000 semifinal after beating fellow Czech Karolina Muchova 6-3, 6-0.
Bartunkova stamped her authority on the quarterfinal by racing to 5-0 against her seventh-seeded opponent. It was the 20-year-old Bartunkova’s third career win against a top 10-ranked opponent. ___

articles.title_orig: “We need to see China as it actually is” – China Daily hosts ‘Vision China’ in London
articles.title_zh: “We need to see China as it actually is” – China Daily hosts ‘Vision China’ in London
articles.content_orig:
Intended to showcase vibrant and vivid examples of people-to-people links, China Daily organised a ‘Vision China’ event, held at the global headquarters of the Institution of Civil Engineers in central London, on September 17, with the theme, ‘Listen to Each Other, Open New Horizons’.
With opening addresses by Qu Yingpu, publisher and editor-in-chief of China Daily, and Zhao Fei, chargé d’affaires ad interim of the Chinese Embassy in London, the event also heard from renowned British Sinologist Frances Wood, who is also a vice president of the Society for Anglo-Chinese Understanding (SACU). For Frances, mutual learning was not just a ‘good-to-have’, but also central to her nearly 35 years of work at the British Library, which involved the conservation and digitisation of some 7,000 complete manuscripts and 6,000 fragments of ancient scrolls from Dunhuang, in northwest China’s Gansu province, dating from the third to the 10th century CE.
Michael Spence, president and provost of University College London (UCL), noted the contributions of the college’s 15,000 Chinese students and its many more Chinese alumni, as well as its role in promoting Chinese language learning in schools across the country. Listing some daunting global challenges – from fighting climate change to governing artificial intelligence – Spence said he does not see any “reasons for pessimism”, because what British and Chinese students, scholars and researchers have already achieved through collaboration is “proof of what is possible”.
Other speakers included Chen Junyan, winner of the second prize at the Leeds International Piano Competition in 2024, Mike Longhurst, a fellow of the Royal Photographic Society, and Richard Trainor, provost of the Rhodes Trust at the University of Oxford.
Also addressing the event was Ondřej Dostál, a member of the European Parliament from Czechia (Czech Republic), who began by noting with reference to his country’s socialist period: “I was born in Czechoslovakia, which was never a colonial power, but always helped the developing countries across the world with technologies and education.”
Referring to how times are changing, he continued: “When I was eight, we had elections and I remember seeing posters: ‘With the Soviet Union. Forever and never otherwise.’ When I was eleven, the Soviet Union was no more.”
Disillusioning experiences followed with the United States and the European Union, however: “I first visited China in 2008 to attend a conference on health law.
“After I was elected to the European Parliament, I decided to visit China again. I had the honour of being the only Member of the European Parliament present at China’s Victory Day parade commemorating the 80th anniversary of the victory over fascism. [On September 3, 2025.] And, just over a month ago, on 15 August, I laid flowers at Chairman Mao’s statue in Shaoshan, and saw, not only in the museum, but also in real life, what China has achieved over a mere three generations.
“I saw the incredible development of China in cities such as Shanghai, Hangzhou, Changsha and Ningbo. I saw how China has become the world’s leader in innovation, patents and high-quality productive forces and in technologies that will shape our future.”
But there is still “an enormous gap between the real China and perceptions of China in the West”.
Dostál thinks there are two reasons for that:
He argues: “We need to understand China as it actually is. Its achievements and its contradictions. Its history and its aspirations. Its government and its people.
“Only when we see China as it actually is, can Europe formulate a China policy based on reality rather than projection.”
We reprint below the text of Mr Dostál’s speech, which has been lightly edited by us. It is preceded by China Daily ’s report of the event, written by its journalists Xing Yi and Wang Huazhong.
Sep 19 ( China Daily ) – Engagement with China fosters a deeper understanding of the country and encourages more people from abroad to visit China, meet its people and experience its culture, said experts in education, art and music on Thursday.
They made the remarks during a Vision China event held at the global headquarters of the Institution of Civil Engineers in central London, the United Kingdom. The event, themed “Listen to Each Other, Open New Horizons”, aimed to inspire its audiences to engineer a cultural bridge to overcome boundaries with an inclusive mindset.
The London edition of Vision China followed a recent phone conversation between President Xi Jinping and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. It underscored their consensus on the importance of communication and exchanges in developing bilateral relations.
During the phone call, Xi urged China and the UK to seek common ground while reserving differences and make their mutually beneficial cooperation even stronger. Burnham expressed the UK’s readiness to advance bilateral cooperation across all fields and strengthen people-to-people exchanges.
Qu Yingpu, publisher and editor-in-chief of China Daily, which hosted Thursday’s event, said via video call that “by heeding this shared vision, China and the UK can also encourage the wider international community to bridge differences and work together”.
Even though advancements in technology have made communication quicker and easier, “we still need closer exchanges to break preconceptions that often shape how we see one another”, Qu said.
He called on everyone to see, meet and listen, in order to build better understanding through empathy and carry forward friendly relations. “We need to open new horizons for international cooperation and development, and make greater contributions to building a community with a shared future for humanity,” Qu added.
Zhao Fei, charge d’affaires ad interim of the Chinese embassy in the UK, also gave a speech.
Ondrej Dostal, a member of the European Parliament representing Czechia, said that he has traveled to China several times and has seen how the nation has effectively become the world’s most significant innovator and producer, which is more than mere technological prowess.
For many people in the West, “perceptions have simply failed to keep pace with reality” and there is an “enormous gap between the real China and perceptions of China”, he said, referring to the intentional smearing of China in Western political discourse and media, which is designed to prevent engagement with the country and contain its rise.
“Therefore, a great deal of work is ahead of us in explaining China’s vision to Europe and to the world,” Dostal said, noting that Europe and China face “too many common challenges to allow misunderstandings to define our relationship”.
“Only when we see China as it actually is can Europe formulate a China policy based on reality, rather than projection. Only then can we move beyond outdated stereotypes and manufactured threat narratives. Only then can we move beyond rivalry and finally embrace partnership — and, I hope, friendship,” he added.
For renowned British Sinologist Frances Wood, mutual learning is not just a good-to-have, but also central to her 30 years of work at the British Library, which involves the conservation and digitization of some 7,000 complete manuscripts and 6,000 fragments of ancient scrolls from Dunhuang, Northwest China’s Gansu province, dating from the third century to the 10th century.
She recalled how British and Chinese conservators worked together to repair the fragments, forging friendships and a family-like bond along the way.
“After decades of hard work, we had a lot to show for it — over 7,000 ‘new’ manuscripts transformed from ‘debris’, and the publishing of a series of academic books,” Wood said.
For Chen Junyan, winner of the second prize at the Leeds International Piano Competition in 2024, listening is not a metaphor. “It is what we do,” she said, adding that music education in Shanghai and London taught her that listening helps broaden one’s horizons.

articles.title_orig: Chico State Agriculture Professor Seeks to Deliver Virtual Fences and Real-World Learning
articles.title_zh: Chico State Agriculture Professor Seeks to Deliver Virtual Fences and Real-World Learning
articles.content_orig:
It was mechanical engineering student Ethan Welge’s first time at the University Farm . He trudged onto the muddy, mucky Dairy Unit pasture on this September morning to pilot “Leonard,” a robodog.
The cows were curious. They herded around the mechanical creature—with its spinning LiDAR laser light mounted on its chin—to sniff and size up this little thing in their midst.
“That’s kind of amazing how interested they are,” Welge said, while carefully maneuvering Leonard among the herd.
The exercise was part of agriculture professor Italo Lima’s preparation for a new research project that will use GPS-enabled collars to create virtual fences.
Lima is one of two Chico State faculty members this year to earn a highly competitive CSU Growth in Undergraduate Innovation, Discovery and Engagement (GUIDE) grant. Professor Deserea Langley of the Ethnic, Gender, and Queer Studies Department received $80,000 on a collaboration with Cal Poly Humboldt Native American Studies to increase undergraduate research opportunities and experiential education for Indigenous students. In all, the CSU awarded 26 grants to 18 schools for 2026-27.
Lima received a $40,000 GUIDE grant for “Smart Grazing and Virtual Reality to Improve Organic Dairy Farming and Student Learning.” He’ll hire six undergraduates as researchers this year, and collar dairy cows at the University Farm as part of a virtual fencing experiment. He’ll use the grant money to buy his own robodog, equipped with technology to monitor behavior, health, and location of the cows, as well as pay stipends to the new student researchers.
“The big challenge is grazing management,” Lima said. “Grazing is dynamic. Physical fencing is not. The number of animals grazing changes, the animals change, the forage changes, everything changes over a year or even over a week because of the weather. So why can’t the fence also change?”
Virtual fencing could give livestock producers flexibility. Since the late 19 th century, most U.S. ranchers have used barbed wire to fence in livestock. While effective in keeping cattle enclosed, it can be expensive to install, maintain, and, of course, difficult to reposition. Moreover, barbed wire fencing harms wildlife. A 2006 study published in Wildlife Society Bulletin estimated that every two and a half miles of barbed wire fencing was responsible for killing one deer, elk, or pronghorn a year.
Cost also is an issue with virtual collars, which run upwards of $240 apiece, but prices are expected to drop if or when the technology scales, Lima said.
Using GPS-enabled collars, Lima and his students will draw virtual boundaries across a pasture on smartphones. When a cow crosses a virtual border, its collar will first emit a warning sound. If the cow continues to wander, the collar delivers an “electric stimulus.” The boundary can later be redrawn to move cattle to other grazing areas.
The yearlong experiment will deploy 25 commercial collars to study forage disappearance, grazing distribution, and how cattle adapt to the technology. Lima sees the cows’ response as a research question in itself.
“Part of our research is not only understanding the technology side, but understanding how the animals perceive this technology, how they behave with this technology, and how they adapt and adjust,” he said.
Collars that track cattle location and behavior could have far-reaching benefits for dairy farmers and ranchers. Instead of driving to a distant pasture to check on a herd, a producer could look at a phone to see where cattle are.
“There’s no way to measure how this can change your life,” Lima said.
For students, the project offers something difficult to replicate in a classroom: responsibility for gathering and interpreting their own real-world information.
“Here they’ll be able to build their own data set,” Lima said. “They’ll be able to get their own information. They’ll be able to see things happening in action.”
The six undergraduate researchers will contribute a combined 600 hours to the project, collecting GPS and pasture data and recording cattle behavior with 360-degree cameras. Lima plans to turn the footage and research into virtual reality (VR) instructional materials that could eventually reach hundreds of Chico State students annually.
Lima envisions sharing the materials with other CSU agricultural programs, particularly campuses where students have limited access to livestock.
Lima hopes the project extends beyond a single grant—producing data for larger studies, giving students experience with precision agriculture, and sharing findings with livestock producers.
“Success for me is not finishing the grant,” he said. “It’s more about continuing.”
Michael Drummond is Chico State’s media relations coordinator. He is a Pulitzer Prize finalist, a former war correspondent, author of “Renegades of the Empire,” and enjoys surfing and fishing.

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Isaias live updates: Gulf Coast braces for dangerous storm
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Isaias live updates: Gulf Coast braces for dangerous storm
articles.content_orig:
⛈️🌊 Track the storm, check your local risk and get more detailed timing from meteorologists in the CNN Weather app
Hurricane Isaias is expected to strengthen significantly over Thursday and Friday. Even if it weakens slightly before landfall, the storm will remain dangerous along the Gulf Coast.
Hurricane Isaias is due to make landfall late Friday night into Saturday as a strong Category two storm. A state of emergency has been declared across Florida and Alabama.
All hurricanes are dangerous, but their impacts aren't always created equal. Meteorologist Chris Warren explains how storm size and storm strength influence the impacts communities experience before, during and after landfall.
To help people prepare for hurricanes, scientists studied 40 tropical cyclones and found storm surge hits in eight ways.
Hurricane Isaias is predicted to landfall very close to where Category 2 Hurricane Sally pushed ashore in September 2020, but the outcome won’t be identical.
Isaias is expected to accelerate toward the coast and weaken some before pushing inland as a Category 1 or 2. Sally, on the other hand, moved sluggishly and intensified as it pushed ashore. That means Sally’s strong winds and heavy rainfall battered the coast for longer than Isaias’ will.
Storm surge is where the two hurricanes could share a common trait.
Sally’s combination of surge and tides reached 5 to 7 feet above ground level in Baldwin County, Alabama, and Escambia and Santa Rosa counties in Florida, according to the National Hurricane Center. The predicted storm surge for Isaias along the Alabama coast and the western Florida Panhandle is the exact same.
What places take the brunt of Isaias’ most damaging surge could also differ from what happened during Sally depending on the hurricane’s precise track.
Storm surge is when a storm’s winds pile up ocean water and push it deeper inland than it belongs.
The Gulf Coast typically sees higher levels of surge than other US coastlines and it all has to do with the terrain under the water.
Just as land has different elevations, so does the ocean floor. That terrain is called its bathymetry.
The Gulf is quite shallow for significant span leading up to the US coastline. This means the powerful winds of storms like Isaias push water up closer to the surface instead of remaining untouched in deeper areas.
The more water that piles up, the more that can come ashore as surge.
Gulf Shores Mayor Robert Craft officially asked the Alabama Emergency Management Agency to grant his request for a mandatory evacuation for non-residents and residents living in low lying, flood prone areas via Governor Kay Ivey’s authority.
The mayor has already instituted a voluntary evacuation of non-residents, the limit of his authority.
He made the official mandatory evacuation ask to the Alabama EMA yesterday and was “given a ‘no’ answer,” Craft tells CNN. He is making that request again today.
Craft’s biggest worry are significant impacts from storm surge and that if the evacuation order comes too late, evacuees could get stuck on roads and highways attempting to make their way out.
While the matchup between college football heavyweights No. 2 Georgia and No. 6 Alabama is still slated to kick off at 6:30 p.m. CT in Tuscaloosa on Saturday, ESPN’s College GameDay show has been moved indoors “due to expected inclement weather” amid impacts from Hurricane Isaias, ESPN announced today.
The show will now air from inside the Coleman Coliseum on the University of Alabama’s campus and no overnight camping will be allowed for those looking to attend the broadcast, the university said .
For the game itself, Alabama Athletics says it continues to closely monitor the weather forecast ahead of the game “with the safety and well-being of the student-athletes, coaches, staff and fans as our highest priority.”
Tornadoes are possible anywhere from Mobile, Alabama, to Tallahassee, Florida, as Isaias approaches the shore and makes landfall Friday night into Saturday morning.
As Isaias’ rainbands reach land, they’ll transport moist air from the Gulf and set the stage for some tornadoes.
Tornadoes from tropical systems can pop up with little notice but tend to be short-lived.
Level 2 of 5 risks of severe thunderstorms are in place for parts of the Gulf Coast and Southeast for late Friday and Saturday, according to the Storm Prediction Center. These quick tornadoes are the main severe threat. See the graphics below for the main areas at risk.
Saturday’s severe thunderstorm risk, with tornadoes as the main threat:
The Pensacola International Airport is scheduled to close its terminal to commercial operations Friday morning, according to a city news release. The airport will close its runways at 6 p.m. Friday evening.
All Okaloosa County airports will close Thursday evening, including Destin-Fort Walton Beach. The county is “asking all out-of-town visitors to evacuate from the forecast area of impacts” by 8 p.m. Wednesday.
All trains along the Amtrak Mardi Gras Service line, which runs between New Orleans, Louisiana and Mobile, Alabama, are cancelled through Sunday due to flood gate closures in New Orleans in preparation for Hurricane Isaias, the Southern Rail Commission announced .
Additionally, Amtrak has suspended its Crescent line train service between New Orleans and Atlanta, the commission said. Services are expected to resume on Monday.
Hurricane Isaias’ winds increased from 35 mph to 70 mph in 24 hours which exactly meets the criteria for rapid intensification.
This satellite time-lapse from Tuesday night to Wednesday night shows thunderstorms bubbling up within Isaias during this intensification period. Isaias continued to rapidly intensify into a hurricane overnight Wednesday.
This animation uses infrared imagery which depicts the most intense thunderstorms near the center of Isaias in purple and white.
Storm surge warnings along the Gulf Coast expanded to include more of Florida late Thursday morning.
The warnings now span from the mouth of the Mississippi River in southeastern Louisiana to the Suwannee River in Florida’s Big Bend region.
The worst of the storm surge will occur around landfall east of Isaias’ center, so the storm’s exact track will be crucial.
Landfall is currently expected somewhere near the Alabama-Florida border Friday night or early Saturday morning, but that location will likely wobble over the next day or so.
Isaias is a Category 1 hurricane with sustained winds of 85 mph, according to the National Hurricane Center’s 10 a.m. CT update. That’s an increase of 5 mph from just three hours ago and shows that the hurricane is starting to bulk up again.
Isaias continues to battle some storm-disrupting winds in the atmosphere and dry air that led to its brief strength plateau earlier this morning. But it’s still forecast to reach Category 2 strength this evening and peak as a high-end Category 2 with 110 mph winds overnight Thursday or Friday morning.
Mandatory evacuation orders have been issued for parts of Gulf and Okaloosa counties on the northwest Florida coastline. Walton County has issued a voluntary evacuation notice for low-lying areas.
Governor Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency for 25 counties across the state on Tuesday. Pensacola Mayor D.C. Reeves also issued an emergency declaration for city.
Multiple counties are closing their offices beginning either Thursday or Friday, including Escambia , Okaloosa , Washington and Calhoun counties.
The sun has come up to reveal Hurricane Isaias and its swirling clouds above the Gulf’s record-warm water.
True color satellite imagery shows us what a storm looks like with the naked eye from space — think of it as what you’d see if you were on the space station.
But you need sunlight to illuminate the clouds and use this imagery. The storm’s bright white clouds appear in the loop as the satellite captures the moment of this morning’s sunrise.

articles.title_orig: From coast to coast: China’s national day marked in Canada
articles.title_zh: From coast to coast: China’s national day marked in Canada
articles.content_orig:
In the following article, Arnold August, Canadian author, political activist and an active contributor to the work of Friends of Socialist China, takes the recent celebration of the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China as an occasion to assess the prospects for both enhanced bilateral relations and greater people-to-people friendship.
This year’s anniversary found echoes right across the vast land of Canada, from Prince Edward Island in the Atlantic to British Columbia facing the Pacific. Arnold lays particular emphasis on the role of Canada’s Chinese community, who, often in the face of discrimination and oppression, have, particularly since mass settlement began in the 1850s, made such an important contribution to building and developing their adopted nation and at the same time acting as the sturdy bridge of friendship back to their ancestral homeland.
He also assesses the recent positive developments in the relations between Canada and China, following a somewhat grim period, and especially since Prime Minister Mark Carney’s visit in January this year. Ambassador to Canada Wang Di provides a comprehensive survey of the present state of the relationship in an article contributed to a special supplement of The Hill Times . The Ambassador’s article is reproduced in full in the body of the article below.
Finally, Arnold notes: “Should this new situation mean we should still be careful not to overestimate Canada’s current positive role, since there are always pressures to throw a wrench into this present trend? Yes, it is right to be cautious. On the other hand, should one underestimate the Carney government’s role? The answer to this is no.”
More than 400 guests attended the Chinese Embassy in Canada’s 77th anniversary national day reception on September 24, 2026, held in the capital Ottawa at the iconic Fairmont Château Laurier.
Prince Edward Island (PEI) is one of Canada’s easternmost provinces, situated on the Atlantic coast. This small island is 980 km from Ottawa. Yet the Chinese overseas community there, whose settlement began as early as 1850 amid racist discrimination by the then Canadian government, was well represented at the celebration. The Chinese Society of Prince Edward Island posted on their Facebook account:
“The Chinese Society of Prince Edward Island (CSPEI) was honoured to attend the National Day reception hosted by the Embassy of China in Canada. It was a valuable opportunity to reconnect with old friends, meet new partners, and share how our volunteers bring people together in PEI. We are grateful for the warm conversations, encouragement, and continued support. We’re bringing that energy back to the Island as we prepare for CSPEI’s Mid-Autumn Festival celebration this Saturday [September 26].”
The CSPEI representative at the Ottawa event, Mengyun Candice Chen, posted on her social media: “When you live far from home [China], it means a lot to know there is a place you can turn to for support.” Furthermore, on the eve of the October 1 national day, the CSPEI was instrumental, along with the mayor of PEI’s capital, Charlottetown, in proudly raising the five star red Chinese flag at City Hall.
On October 4, during Golden Week (October 1–7), the CSPEI visited Stratford Elementary School in the province’s capital to highlight Chinese culture, with the Chinese national flag clearly on display.
From the other coast, on the Pacific Ocean, Ali Feiz, from Burnaby (near Vancouver), 3,552 km from Ottawa, was not only present in the nation’s capital at the event, but, as usual on such occasions, made a very important contribution. Ali Feiz has visited and reported on Xinjiang seven times and is one of Canada’s main voices against disinformation about this autonomous region of the People’s Republic. He also posted a photograph with Canadian Senator Victor Oh, the first male Chinese Canadian senator, appointed in 2013, who has consistently advocated for the rights of Chinese Canadians and constructive bilateral engagement. Ali Feiz published this on social media:
In a period marked by renewed dialogue between Canada and China, the Honourable Victor Oh, a prominent figure in the Chinese Canadian community, has emerged as a leading voice for pragmatic engagement. As the first male Chinese Canadian senator, appointed in 2013, he has consistently advocated for the rights of Chinese Canadians and for constructive bilateral engagement. His recent firsthand visit to Xinjiang and his address at the 77th anniversary celebration of the People’s Republic of China in Ottawa illustrates a consistent approach that prioritizes direct observation and people-centered development over distant speculation. In September 2026, the Honourable Victor Oh visited China and traveled to Xinjiang. During his time in Xinjiang, he visited a range of locations. In his address, the Honourable Victor Oh told the story of asking three Uyghur children in a Urumqi school what they wanted to be when they grew up. Without hesitation, they answered, “I want to be a doctor.” This moment, he said, crystallized for him the true measure of development. It is not about abstract statistics but about giving the next generation confidence and hope, ensuring that every hardworking ordinary person can see a tangible future.
On the speech by Honourable Rob Oliphant, Parliamentary Secretary to the Canadian Minister of Foreign Affairs, Ali Feiz pointed out in his X account the following – (it is particularly useful to note Oliphant’s comment on the One China Policy, which is always under pressure):
In his remarks, Honourable Rob Oliphant acknowledged the remarkable achievements of the Chinese people over the past 77 years while also addressing the need for honest dialogue between Canada and China. He stated that Canada will honour and stand up for the One China policy. He emphasised that a mature relationship is built on mutual respect, direct communication, and a shared commitment to addressing global challenges such as climate change, public health, and economic stability. The speech was notable for its balance. Honourable Rob Oliphant highlighted the importance of people-to-people ties, the contributions of Chinese Canadians to the fabric of Canadian society and the value of educational, cultural, and economic exchanges. Honourable Rob Oliphant’s address comes at a pivotal moment in Canada-China relations. Earlier this year, PM Mark Carney’s visit to China brought new momentum to bilateral ties, with both governments describing efforts to build what has been called a new strategic partnership. As Canada and China navigate a pivotal moment in their relationship, the speech served as a reminder that diplomacy is not merely about managing differences but about building bridges. His words will likely be remembered as a significant contribution to that ongoing effort.
In addition to Rob Oliphant, in attendance were Kody Blois, Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister; Deputy Minister of International Trade, Glenn Purves; Deputy Minister of Canadian Heritage, Francis Bilodeau; and more than a dozen Members of Parliament and Senators, Members of the diplomatic corps, and representatives of Chinese enterprises.
HE Wang Di, the PRC’s Ambassador to Canada, and his wife Liu Yuyu were the hosts. Ambassador Wang addressed the gathering, noting that October 1 this year marks the 77th anniversary of the founding of the PRC, and this year also marks the 105th anniversary of the founding of the Communist Party of China (CPC), and the start of China’s 15th Five-Year Plan (2026—2030). Under CPC leadership, the Chinese people are advancing with confidence toward the goals of building China into a great modern socialist country in all respects and realising the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.
On September 30, the embassy published a special supplement in Ottawa-based The Hill Times celebrating the 77th national day. Ambassador Wang Di contributed a bylined article

articles.title_orig: Trump says US will not attack Iran before midterm elections in November
articles.title_zh: Trump says US will not attack Iran before midterm elections in November
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump announced Thursday that the U.S. military "will not be attacking Iran" in the leadup to November's midterm elections.
"We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran. I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect, with Oil flowing in Record Numbers of Barrels through the Hormuz Strait (22 Million Barrels, last night alone, with not one barrel coming from, or going to, Iran!), we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
"IRAN WILL NOT HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON!" the president also declared.
U.S. Central Command said Thursday that "in recent months, U.S. forces have supported the shipment of over 1.25 billion barrels of crude oil from Gulf partners and through the Strait of Hormuz.
"In contrast, Iran has not shipped any barrels because of America's ironclad blockade on Iranian ports," it wrote on X.
CENTCOM revealed earlier this week that 130 ships have been redirected as part of the blockade.
"The U.S. military remains intensely focused on this mission, Adm. Brad Cooper, CENTCOM commander, said in a statement. "We will swiftly act against any vessels trying to run the blockade. Our forces are highly trained, professional, and lethal."
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) said Thursday that a crude oil tanker has been struck while traveling through the Strait of Hormuz.
The incident, in which the tanker was hit by an "unknown projectile," happened on Wednesday, according to the UKMTO.
"There have been no reported casualties. Damage assessment and environmental impact are unknown at time of report," it added.
A White House official told Fox News on Thursday that "President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States" when asked to respond to reporting about potential strikes against Iran.
The remark comes after The Atlantic, citing two administration officials, reported Wednesday that “The White House has asked the Pentagon to develop strike options against Iranian targets that could be exercised ahead of the midterms.”
“The Commander-in-Chief has all options available at any time. The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing," the White House official said.
"Iran has been decimated, and things will go one of two ways; the easy way or the hard way," the official added.
Fox News' Patrick Ward contributed to this post.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani doubled down Thursday in accusing Israel of waging a genocide in Gaza after being criticized over a statement he released yesterday on the anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks while also being called a "traitor" by anti-Israel protesters.
Mamdani, during the anniversary of the attacks on Wednesday, released a statement saying three years ago, "on that day, Hamas killed more than 1,100 Israelis and abducted 251 others.
"We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss," Mamdani said. "The suffering did not begin nor end that day. It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza, in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians — including more than 21,000 children," he continued.
Mamdani later was heckled by anti-Israel protesters as he attended a vigil for the Oct. 7, 2023, victims, despite being a longtime critic of the Israeli government's actions in Gaza.
"I was proud to attend last night's vigil, as I did last year, to listen to testimonies from family members of those who were killed on Oct. 7 and those who've been killed in the three years since, and all of whom united in a vision for peace and an end to the genocide in Gaza. And when we're speaking of that genocide, we're speaking of one that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians in the last three years," Mamdani told reporters Thursday. "As for those protesting me, I am the mayor of New York City, and this is what I signed up for.
"And I've been very clear, both as a candidate as well as the mayor of our city, of my firm belief that we have to extend human rights to all people and that has to include Palestinians. And that as Americans, we have a special responsibility, given our federal government's complicity in funding so much of the weaponry that has been used over these last three years," Mamdani continued.
"And we also know that when we are commemorating the anniversary, three years of horrific war crimes, three years since Hamas killed more than 1,100 Israelis and abducted hundreds more, three years of an anniversary that has brought unthinkable devastation to so many that also the Israeli government used and continues to use that day, those war crimes, as a justification for an ongoing genocide against Palestinians.
“This is something that has shattered the lives of so many New Yorkers, whether in those who I was standing alongside at the vigil, recounting their own family members who were killed, or reading the testimonies of Palestinians whose family members have been killed, or the then-Palestinian New Yorkers that I met soon after that vigil who shared with me — for example, a Palestinian-Christian nurse here in New York City sharing with me that she lost 17 of her family members when the Israeli military bombed a church," Mamdani said. "It has devastated people's lives across our city."
Fox News Digital's Landon Mion contributed to this post.
U.S. Central Command said it held a meeting Thursday with international shipping partners to discuss the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, where ships continue to be targeted during the U.S.-Iran war.
"Leaders highlighted building momentum for freedom of navigation as commercial traffic flow increases," CENTCOM wrote on X.
"Adm. Brad Cooper, CENTCOM commander, thanked industry leaders and other U.S. government agencies for their continued support and acknowledged the sacrifices made by civilian crews due to unwarranted Iranian attacks," it added.
U.S. Central Command said the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier is returning home to San Diego, California, on Thursday following its "historic deployment to the Middle East" during Operation Epic Fury.
"Over 5,000 Sailors and Marines supported thousands of combat flights and sailed more than 90,000 miles," CENTCOM said on X. "Congratulations on the well-deserved reunion with loved ones!"
The ship spent more than 300 days at sea during the deployment.
“What the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group did, no other carrier strike group has ever done,” Secretary of War Pete Hegseth said Wednesday. “10,000 sorties, 23,000 combat flight hours, almost 4,000 combat sorties, 1.5 million pounds of ordnance dropped on the enemy,” he added.
Fox News Digital's Emma Bussey contributed to this post.
The Saudi General Directorate of Civil Defense said Thursday that buildings in Saudi Arabia’s capital of Riyadh have suffered damage after a ballistic missile was intercepted.
“Shrapnel fallout resulting from the interception of a ballistic missile in Riyadh city caused material damage to a children's nursery and a medical clinic complex,” it wrote on X.
The Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen claimed earlier Thursday that it launched a ballistic missile attack against King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi claimed Thursday that the U.S. military has lost more aircraft during the war than the Congressional Research Service has reported.
"In May, the Congressional Research Service admitted that Iran’s Armed Forces had taken out 42 U.S. military aircraft. Now: 81. Real toll is far higher," Araghchi wrote on X.

articles.title_orig: Search warrants against former prince Andrew were unlawful, court finds
articles.title_zh: Search warrants against former prince Andrew were unlawful, court finds
articles.content_orig:
Judge makes ruling after former prince brought judicial review of operation linked to Jeffrey Epstein investigation
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has won his legal challenge against Thames Valley police over search warrants used to raid his home after they arrested him.
The former prince brought a judicial review of the legality of the force’s actions and those of the central criminal court, which granted the warrants.
On Thursday, Mr Justice Hilliard, sitting at the high court in central London, said Thames Valley police (TVP) had conceded that it obtained the search powers under the wrong statutory provision and ruled that the warrants were unlawful.
The episode is embarrassing for TVP but police believe it will not affect the success of the investigation.
The warrants were issued by an Old Bailey judge on 18 February and Mountbatten-Windsor was subsequently arrested the following day , on his 66th birthday, on suspicion of misconduct in public office.
The arrest followed information that emerged from the Jeffrey Epstein files. It was alleged that when Mountbatten-Windsor was the UK’s trade envoy he shared sensitive information with Epstein, a convicted child sex offender.
Police began searching the former Duke of York’s residence on the Sandringham estate and his former Windsor home, Royal Lodge, on the same day as his arrest. Documentary material and electronic devices were seized.
Hilliard said the search warrants were quashed but police had made an application, which would be heard next year, to retain the seized property on the basis that it would have been lawful to take it under a different statutory provision. Mountbatten-Windsor opposes that application.
The judge said: “The fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring the investigation to an end or mean that the whole of the investigation is unlawful.”
A senior police source said: “It’s not going to bring the investigation to a halt or affect the chances of success.”
They added: “The news media might say the police messed up. But it was the judicial decision [to grant the warrant] that was incorrect.”
TVP have been in discussions with lawyers from the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) about the strength of their case and what evidence they would need for a prosecution.
A TVP spokesperson said: “The agreement that led to the quashing of the warrants relates specifically to a decision made by the court regarding the legal basis for these and is not a judgment on our ongoing investigation.
“We ensured the court was presented with all the necessary information and paperwork to inform their decision, following the correct legal processes throughout.
“We accept the position that the initial court’s decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect and therefore these must be legally quashed.”
Hilliard told the court that the grant of a search warrant under section eight of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act (Pace) 1984 was conditional on the issuing judge being satisfied there were reasonable grounds to suspect that the material sought did not include items subject to legal privilege or special procedure material.
Special procedure material includes documents in possession of a person who acquired them in the course of any trade, business, profession or other occupation – for the purpose of any paid or unpaid office – who holds it subject to an express or implied undertaking to hold it in confidence.
The judge said the presence of legally privileged material was expressly envisaged in the application for the search warrants and that material was likely to be in the possession of Mountbatten-Windsor “who had acquired or created it in circumstances which would make it special procedure material”. He concluded that a lawful warrant could only have been issued under section nine of Pace.
Nick Vamos, the former head of special crime at the CPS, said: “Given the technical nature of the errors revealed today, I expect the crown court to rule in due course that the police can keep the material, or at least as much of it as they would have been entitled to seize in the first place, so they may not ultimately pay much of a price beyond today’s red faces.”
Late last year, King Charles stripped his brother of his right to be a prince and of his dukedom over his association with Epstein.
Mountbatten-Windsor receives an annual stipend, the amount of which has not been disclosed, from King Charles’s private funds, but a palace source told reporters it had been made clear this should not be used to fund the judicial review .

articles.title_orig: Canadian author Anne Carson wins literature Nobel for 'bold and inventive' works that blend genres
articles.title_zh: Canadian author Anne Carson wins literature Nobel for 'bold and inventive' works that blend genres
articles.content_orig:
The Canadian poet and essayist’s work often blends verse, prose, dialogue and translation in a genre-defying mix
The winner of this year’s Nobel Prize in Literature is Canada’s Anne Carson, an essayist and classicist who brings a modern twist to mysticism and antiquity in her writings about love, desire and despair.
The 76-year-old won “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature”, the Swedish Academy said on Thursday.
Carson is widely known for her translations of classical Greek literature, which heavily influences her work which ranges from opera librettos to literary criticism and verse novels such as Autobiography of Red from 1998.
Her style ⁠is exemplified in Norma Jeane Baker of Troy from 2019, a performance piece which mixes the ‌stories of Helen of Troy in Euripides’ play Helen and Marilyn Monroe.

articles.title_orig: Scottie Pearman heads to Reno eyeing a World Long Drive title after hitting 486-yard drive
articles.title_zh: Scottie Pearman heads to Reno eyeing a World Long Drive title after hitting 486-yard drive
articles.content_orig:
Imagine hitting a golf ball 486 yards. For Scottie Pearman, smashing the ball far is what he's known for.
"A lot of the time it's about right place, right time and right conditions," Pearman said.
During the last year's World Long Drive Championships, Pearman's 468-yard drive helped elevate him to be the No. 1 player in the world. He accomplished that at 4,678 feet of elevation in La Salle, Colo. Now, he'll try to replicate that performance at Reno's  high attitude. The World Long Drive Championships presented by Caesars will make its first stop in Reno when Wildcreek Golf Course hosts the event for the next three years.
"Reno itself is a great hosting site," Pearman said. "When you think of long drive, you think of numbers that are unattainable by most average golfers. We're talking over 400 yards easily. I'm hoping the wind stays a factor because the way it was blowing I feel bad for everyone that has to hit against me."
The idea of a competition featuring golfers hitting the ball as far as they can began in the 1970s. It's gone through several iterations and name changes, but in 2024 the league became known as the World Long Drive Tour. The tour has four divisions, including the Elite Open, Rise, Senior and Women's with more than 100 competitors across those groups. WLD is made up of many former athletes from across several sports, including the NFL, MLB and NHL.
"A normal driver is probably nine to 10 degrees," Pearman said. "My driver, I keep it set three-to-five degrees. They're basically fishing rods attached to a putter. It is hard to hit. It's high-risk, high-reward. But at the end of the day, fortune favors the bold. You've got to go big or go home."
Pearman has never won the World Long Drive championship. But he knows the importance of being able to take home the coveted belt.
"It's basically our Super Bowl," Pearman said. "Of course everyone wants to win a tournament as the year goes on. But at the end of the day, no one really members who won what other than when you hold that belt over your head."
The 2026 World Long Drive Championship runs from Oct. 15-17. A last-chance qualifier event will be held Oct. 14 before Saturday's championship final. You can purchase tickets here . Golf Channel will produce a national broadcast Dec. 1.

articles.title_orig: Venezuela's Maduro, wife Flores tortured opponents to stay in power, US prosecutors say
articles.title_zh: Venezuela's Maduro, wife Flores tortured opponents to stay in power, US prosecutors say
articles.content_orig:
Fox News national correspondent Bryan Llenas reports from Manhattan federal court as former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro appears for a hearing on narco-terrorism and drug-trafficking charges. Prosecutors allege Maduro led a drug-trafficking organization for over two decades. His attorneys are expected to argue he is immune from prosecution as a head of state and that his capture by U.S. Special Forces was unlawful. The Treasury Department authorized Venezuela to fund Maduro's legal defense.
The United States District Court for the Southern District of New York charged former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores with conspiracy to commit torture to Americans and others, according to a superseding indictment filed Thursday.
Maduro's government, according to the indictment, "presided over a system of repression that relied on violence against political opposition, arbitrary detention, and the torture of detainees, including United States citizens."
The torture included "electric shock, asphyxiation, rape , forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells, and psychological torture, such as threats to harm and kill victims' families, including children," the indictment read.
The charge carries a maximum of life imprisonment if any of the alleged torture resulted in death, and a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison if not.
FAMILIES SUE MADURO IN US, ACCUSE EX-PRESIDENT OF DIRECTING POLICE UNIT TIED TO EXTRAJUDICIAL KILLINGS
Captured Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, appear with their attorneys Barry Pollack and Mark Donnelly at their arraignment in a federal court in New York City on Monday, Jan. 5, 2026. (Jane Rosenberg)
In one incident, the indictment alleges that a U.S. detainee in Venezuela was beaten for days and doused with a noxious liquid that made him vomit, which Venezuelan officers then allegedly made him eat.
WAR CRIMES COURT TURNS 'BLIND EYE' TO TOP WORLD THREATS WHILE TARGETING AMERICANS, TRUMP ADMIN ACCUSES
The detainee, who was allegedly accused of plotting to kill Maduro, was also subjected to electric shock torture to his torso and genitals and injected with a substance that induced seizures.
"On one occasion, CC-3 personally observed Victim-7 being electrocuted; laughed at and taunted Victim-7 during the electric shock; and directed other DGCIM officers in connection with the electric shock," the indictment read.
MADURO'S ALLEGED 'BAG MAN' ALEX SAAB ARRESTED LESS THAN 3 YEARS AFTER BIDEN PARDON: REPORT
After spending eight-and-a-half months at Boleíta Norte prison in Venezuela, the detainee was released and returned to the U.S. in October 2022, according to the indictment.
Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are seen in handcuffs after landing at a Manhattan helipad, escorted by heavily armed Federal agents as they make their way into an armored car en route to a Federal courthouse in Manhattan on January 5, 2026 in New York City. (XNY/Star Max/GC Images)
The indictment alleges Maduro and Flores "inflicted severe physical and mental pain and suffering to repress and punish political opposition, silence dissent and perceived dissent, preserve and protect the power and authority of the members of the conspiracy, and intimidate, harass, and neutralize their opponents, including through kidnappings."
The pair, who face numerous other charges, were arrested in Venezuela in January during Operation Absolute Resolve . Maduro was originally charged with narco-terrorism conspiracy, cocaine importation conspiracy, possession of machine guns and destructive devices, and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices in a 2011 indictment that President Donald Trump's Department of Justice unsealed in 2020.
Flores was then charged in a superseding indictment in January with cocaine importation conspiracy, possession of machine guns and destructive devices and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices. They have pleaded not guilty and face a minimum of 50 years in prison if convicted. A trial is scheduled for June 2027.
EXCLUSIVE: FBI EXTRADITIONS SOAR AS PATEL RAMPS UP FOREIGN OUTREACH, VOWS 'NO SANCTUARY'
Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are seen in handcuffs after landing at a Manhattan helipad, escorted by heavily armed Federal agents as they make their way into an armored car en route to a Federal courthouse in Manhattan on January 5, 2026 in New York City. (XNY/Star Max/GC Images via Getty Images)
Flores appeared in court Thursday for a bond hearing on her motion for release from jail. Her lawyers were requesting home confinement with GPS tracking, citing a heart condition and arguing she does not pose a danger to the community. US District Judge Alvin Hellerstein denied the request.
The U.S. government opposes her release, arguing she poses a flight risk and danger to the public.
Flores' attorneys say she denies the allegations against her, and both she and Maduro have filed motions to dismiss on diplomatic immunity grounds.

articles.title_orig: Feed the Children Marks World Food Day with "It All Begins with Food," Centering Children's Own Words
articles.title_zh: Feed the Children Marks World Food Day with "It All Begins with Food," Centering Children's Own Words
articles.content_orig:
OKLAHOMA CITY, Oct. 8, 2026
OKLAHOMA CITY , Oct. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- On World Food Day, Oct. 16, Feed the Children, a global movement working to end child hunger, is sharing "It All Begins with Food"—a World Food Day awareness effort built on the words of children themselves. Daniela in El Salvador, Halima in Tanzania, Andrew in the Philippines and Bodi in the United States each describe, in their own words, who they hope to become. Their voices are central to Feed the Children's World Food Day observance, appearing across feedthechildren.org , social content and more. The reality behind these stories is urgent: according to UNICEF, one in four children under age 5 worldwide is living in severe child food poverty—181 million children who don't have reliable access to the nutritious food they need to grow, learn and thrive.
Food is the starting point for everything a child can become. When children eat consistently and well, they show up to school ready to learn, they grow into their potential and they begin to imagine and pursue futures that are entirely their own. That's what World Food Day, observed each year on Oct. 16, calls the world to recognize: food isn't just sustenance—it's the foundation of possibility.
"No child should go to bed hungry. No child. Anywhere," said Emily Callahan, president and CEO of Feed the Children. "When children have enough to eat, they show up to school, they stay healthy and they start building the futures they deserve. Ending child hunger is possible—but only if we do it together."
Children Share What Food Makes Possible
Daniela is 9 years old and wants to be a police officer in El Salvador—someone who protects her country and looks out for her family. Half a world away in Tanzania, 12-year-old Halima wants to become a journalist, determined to tell the stories of her village to the world. In the Philippines, 10-year-old Andrew channels a love of math and problem-solving into a dream of becoming an engineer. And in the United States, 9-year-old Bodi is already imagining a future shaped by his love of soccer.
Each child's story reflects countless others across the communities Feed the Children works alongside. Their words speak for themselves. "Food is important to be a good athlete," says Bodi. Andrew is just as direct: "I like eating at school because I get to eat good food with my classmates." In Tanzania, when Halima's family's sweet potato harvest fell short, Feed the Children worked alongside her community to strengthen nutrition while advancing Livelihoods & Resilience programming. The experience helped shape the future she imagines for herself. "I want to study hard, tell the stories of our village, and show how we can achieve great things together," she says.
The scale of the challenge is clear. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, an estimated 645 million people faced hunger in 2025. In the U.S., up to 40% of the food supply goes to waste each year, according to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration—a stark reminder of how much inequity exists within our food system and how much more is possible when communities, partners and donors work together. The data is striking, but the conclusion isn't hopelessness. It's urgency.
Scale of Reach, Depth of Impact
In fiscal year 2025, Feed the Children distributed nearly 78 million meals to nearly 15 million people spanning almost every U.S. state and eight countries: El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Kenya, Malawi, Tanzania, Uganda and the Philippines.
This October, the organization is celebrating the opening of two new Feed the Children Food & Essentials Hub locations: School of Dreams Academy Charter School in Los Lunas, New Mexico and Mater Academy of Nevada East Campus in Las Vegas. The program works directly with school districts to provide students with food, essential household items, personal care products, books and school supplies throughout the school year.
Program-wide in fiscal year 2026, Feed the Children Food & Essentials Hubs reached more than 154,900 students and 58,600 households across 834 schools in 11 states—providing more than 686,000 meals and more than $6.7 million in food, essentials, books and school supplies. The results speak to what consistent access makes possible: 87% of participating school districts reported improvements in student confidence and attendance, and nearly two-thirds of caregivers said the program helped reduce the need to cut or skip meals for their children.
This World Food Day, Feed the Children invites supporters to explore and read the stories of children whose own words are at the heart of "It All Begins with Food" because when children have the food and support they need most today, they can begin to imagine who they will become tomorrow. Together, we can help create a world where no child goes to bed hungry.
Feed the Children is a global movement working to end childhood hunger in the U.S. and around the world. Together with communities, the organization provides food, essentials and opportunities to children and families who need them most so every child can survive and thrive. Learn more at feedthechildren.org .
Create a world where no child goes to bed hungry.
