articles.title_orig: Congressional candidate says she was raped while repairing campaign signs
articles.title_zh: Congressional candidate says she was raped while repairing campaign signs
articles.content_orig:
EDITOR’S NOTE: This story contains graphic details of sexual violence.
A US congressional candidate in Arizona, Bernadette Greene-Placentia, says she was raped by two men while she was repairing one of her campaign signs.
Greene-Placentia said it happened August 14 around 2 or 3 a.m. in the Phoenix suburb of Sun City, according to an incident report from the Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office shared by her campaign.
Greene-Placentia reported the incident to the sheriff’s office more than two weeks later on August 31, according to the report.
“When it first happened, I didn’t want to tell anybody,” she told The New York Times on Wednesday. “I was embarrassed that I couldn’t defend myself,” she said.
CNN has sought comment from Greene-Placentia. The sheriff’s office is investigating the case, it said Wednesday.
The Democratic candidate for Arizona’s 8th congressional district, which includes parts of Phoenix and nearby areas including Sun City, was out putting up and fixing political signage and was hit in the back of her head by two unknown men while walking back to her vehicle, the incident report says. Greene-Placentia lost consciousness and does not recall how she was hit in the head or how many times, according to the report, which says she and investigators have not been able to determine the exact location of the attack.
She woke up to the pain of one of the men concluding intercourse while holding her down, according to the report. She “described having bruises on her arms from being held down.”
The other man then raped her, the report says. She said she also recalls seeing her feet as she fought back by kicking.
Greene-Placentia does not remember what the men looked like or what they were wearing, according to the report.
“She only recalled one of them wearing black boots and having small feet,” the incident report reads.
She recalled to investigators that one of the men said “democratic b*tch” at some point during the incident, the report states. But, on Wednesday, she said she could not be sure what she had heard, according to The New York Times .
The incident report says that she did not take any pictures of the bruises on her body or the bump of her head following the incident.
She told deputies that “immediately after the sexual assault, she went home and took three showers and a bath.” Greene-Placentia did not go to a hospital or get a Sexual Assault Nurse Examiner (SANE) exam.
“I asked Bernadette if there was any DNA left on her clothing, which she stated she has washed the clothes since then,” an investigator wrote in the incident report.
Both men remain “truly unknown,” the report adds.
“I look back and it’s like, why didn’t I go to the hospital?” she told CNN affiliate KNXV . “I’d always considered myself a strong person, and so I was embarrassed.”
The Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office followed up with Greene-Placentia on September 1, and she provided more details of her injuries.
She explained she was struck on the left side on the back of her head, which had a significant bump on it. She also had three vertical bruises that appeared to be in the shape of a hand on her left arm, according to the report.
Greene-Placentia also stated she experienced vaginal bleeding for two to three days following the assault. She also told the sheriff’s office her assailants may have been White males.
“She did not recall if the male subjects left by foot or got into a vehicle,” the incident report says.
According to the report, she did not tell anyone of the incident until two to three days later, when she talked to her husband, Alexander Placentia, and two campaign staff members.
After the initial reluctance to speak out, Greene-Placentia felt she would be a “hypocrite” if she didn’t go public, she told The New York Times.
“I don’t want my campaign to be about this,” she said to the newspaper, “but women need to know it’s OK to come forward.”
“Speaking publicly about what happened has been incredibly difficult for Bernadette,” campaign spokesperson Craig Beckman said in a statement to CNN on Wednesday. “She chose to share her story because she knows many survivors struggle in silence, and she hopes that by speaking about her experience, others will know they are not alone.”
Greene-Placentia’s political opponent, incumbent US Rep. Abraham Hamadeh, said in a statement to the Times that law enforcement should “investigate these serious allegations thoroughly, including finding all possible camera footage of the time and place, in order to prosecute the crime to the fullest extent of the law.”
Greene-Placencia told KNXV she hopes speaking out will help other survivors.
“I believe very strongly in women’s bodily autonomy, and I was angry that these men used their physical size to take that autonomy from me,” Greene-Placentia said. “Speaking up was me taking it back.”
Help is available : For help in the US, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673 or chat 24/7 on online.rainn.org .
CNN’s Michael Williams and Andy Rose contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: A year into Trump’s peace plan, Netanyahu stands in the way of rebuilding
articles.title_zh: A year into Trump’s peace plan, Netanyahu stands in the way of rebuilding
articles.content_orig:
Hamas operatives largely keep a low profile, but armed men still appear in the streets at night
In the three years since the October 7 massacre, the state of Israel and the region as a whole have changed beyond recognition. The same applies to the Gaza Strip. According to the most recent available satellite imagery, roughly 80% of all buildings in Gaza have been damaged or destroyed during the war.
Israeli forces currently control 63% of Gaza's territory. In the remaining 37%, some two million Gazans live in the densely populated city centers and tent cities across the Strip. And life there is uncertain, with many fearing a resumption of the fighting as Hamas refuses to concede power and disarm.
The prevailing mood is one of frustration and despair. For three years, residents have waited for the war to end and for the technocratic committee meant to run Gaza to begin operating there. That moment still seems distant. "Three years have passed with people hoping that the war would end, but it hasn't, and we are still stuck," one woman in Gaza told i24NEWS. "As you know, people have been living in tents for three years, and this is extremely difficult."
Tension rose in the days leading up to the anniversary, as many families stockpiled food in case of an emergency. The fear that a major military operation could see the IDF take over what remains of the Strip has not gone away. "We don't feel stable, and honestly, we don't feel that there is any real hope for peace," she said.
Hamas operatives largely keep a low profile, but armed men still appear in the streets at night. Residents often cannot tell whether these men belong to Hamas or to one of the armed groups operating from behind the Yellow Line. "To be honest with you, we don't know who they are," she said.
Residents also say Hamas finances itself in part by imposing various taxes on residents and merchants, which some describe as extortion. "Here, we know very well that Hamas must hand over all its weapons," the Gazan said. "The people of Gaza want to get rid of Hamas and its rule, so that this situation we are living through and suffering from can finally come to an end."
Food and basic goods are available, the woman said. "There is no famine at all. Food and other goods are available, but not everyone has the means to buy them. The poor and those who don't have jobs depend on free aid and on groups that cook free food in the streets and distribute it to them."
Work in Gaza is scarce. Many of the available jobs in the various NGOs operating in the Strip are subject to Hamas's approval, as it decides who can get hired. If you're not affiliated with Hamas, chances are you won't find work.
Despite criticism in Western and Arab capitals, where Israeli plans to encourage emigration from Gaza have been branded "ethnic cleansing," the woman who spoke with i24NEWS said she hopes to leave at the first opportunity. "I intend not to return," she said.

articles.content_orig:

Persistent AI-agent world on Base to become the operating business of the public company
LAS VEGAS, Oct. 08, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Third Life World, LLC ("Third Life World"), the developer of a persistent online world where AI agents own land, build, work and trade, today announced that it has signed a definitive Control Share Purchase Agreement with Transglobal Management Group, Inc. (OTC: TMGI) ("TMGI" or the "Company") and its controlling shareholder, Marc Angell.
Under the agreement, Third Life World acquires the voting control of the Company which expects to make Third Life World's platform its core operating business.
Third Life World acquires the Series A Preferred control block which holds a majority of the voting rights.
TMGI will create a new Series B Preferred Stock to assist with this purchase.
At closing, Marc Angell will step down from his officer positions at TMGI. He will remain available to the Company as a consultant to support a smooth transition.
New management and board designees will be named by Third Life World in accordance with applicable notice and filing requirements.
Closing is subject to customary conditions, including transfer-agent processing and the filing of the Series B Certificate of Designation with the Florida Secretary of State.
About the Third Life World platform
Third Life World ( thirdlifeworld.xyz ) is a live, persistent world built on the Base blockchain. Players create AI agents that claim land, construct buildings, gather resources, earn ranks and trade on an in-world marketplace, with activity settled in the platform's native currency, $AMETA. The world runs continuously on a timed "tick" cycle, so agents keep working and the economy keeps moving even when their owners are offline.
As of September 14, 2026, the platform reported 4,780 players , 5,004 AI agents and 2,111 of 5,625 land parcels claimed , with 25 building types available. The platform earns revenue through a 1% fee on in-world transactions, agent creation, premium agent subscriptions and land and building sales. It also offers an API that lets outside developers connect their own AI agents to the world.
Growth plan Over the next six months, the Company plans to:
Launch Version 3 of the world, adding map visibility, NPC movement, vehicles and deeper customization;
Release mobile apps on the Apple App Store and Google Play;
Publish public API documentation and onboard outside developers and partners; and
Grow toward its target of 50,000 users.
Management commentary "Taking control of a public company gives Third Life World a platform to scale," said Jorge Guinovart, Managing Member of Third Life World, LLC. "We've built a live world where AI agents already own land, build and trade around the clock. With TMGI, we can bring that to a much larger audience, fund mobile and Version 3, and give our community a transparent public company to follow."
"We are pleased to hand TMGI to a team with a live product and a clear plan, and I look forward to supporting the transition." said Marc Angell, outgoing CEO of TMGI.
About Transglobal Management Group, Inc. Transglobal Management Group, Inc. (OTCID: TMGI) is a publicly traded company listed on the OTC Markets Basic platform, headquartered in St. Petersburg, Florida.
About Third Life World, LLC Third Life World, LLC is a Nevada limited liability company based in Las Vegas. It builds and operates Third Life World, a persistent AI-agent world and economy on the Base blockchain. Learn more at thirdlifeworld.xyz and on X at @ThirdLifeWorld .

articles.title_orig: ‘The Floating World’ by Ben Eastham, Reviewed
articles.title_zh: ‘The Floating World’ by Ben Eastham, Reviewed
articles.content_orig:
For all its suspicion of the contemporary artworld and its machinations, the art critic’s debut novel remains surprisingly sincere about art itself
The unnamed narrator of Ben Eastham’s debut novel, The Floating World , is, like Eastham himself , an art critic. Grieving his recently deceased wife, he feels lost while teaching at a school where the students refer to him as ‘Doctor Pissington’. Then a friend offers him a job back in the artworld. He is to work on ‘The Floating World’, which is ‘a gated community beneath a giant dome on a desert island’ being built by a tech billionaire for the wealthiest as a refuge from climate crisis and political collapse. Our morally conflicted protagonist is hired to conduct research for an art exhibition marking the island’s inauguration. The novel negotiates the contradiction of inhabiting a contemporary artworld sustained by the good intentions of art workers who align themselves with beauty and virtue, while depending on the very forces their work purports to resist.
It opens with the narrator, in Ireland, on the verge of writing, before disappearing into his recollections, and eventually returns to the point at which the story is being written (more on which later). Grief provides its emotional landscape: the narrator’s reality is shot through with the frenetic despair that comes with the sudden loss of his wife. His grief gradually becomes entangled with the project of ‘The Floating World’ and the people making it, forcing a confrontation with the loss he has been carrying. It is in such experiences that resist ordinary expression that art becomes most meaningful: a painting, for example, that is ‘a truth that didn’t need explaining. No aristocrats, no symbolism, no lies. A painting clear as love’; and another, when the narrator’s friend likens the experience of pregnancy to a painting they once saw in a museum, in which ‘The colours are stronger and brighter, there’s a texture. It’s like breaking through a screen, the world feels bigger, like it can’t be contained.’
Eastham is at his most sensitive when criticism itself becomes inadequate. There is a pleasing irony in an art critic writing about an art critic for whom, and for the artists around him, the most profound encounters with art seem to occur precisely when interpretation fails. While Eastham is tender in his descriptions of art, his acute observations of the people surrounding it can be lacerating. He has a formidable talent for summoning up a character – or skewering one – in a sentence. One woman possesses ‘the erotic hauteur of an academic who in her youth danced beneath filtered spotlights at psychedelic happenings’. Another, ‘a woman in those oversized metal-rimmed spectacles designed to signal to civilians that the wearer is an intellectual’. Eastham is exacting not only when it comes to how people appear, but also about the identities they are trying, sometimes desperately, to project. Despite the grieving anguish of its narrator, it is his wry, deadpan humour that carries the novel. There is a dryly comic sparring match with a ‘philanthropist’ who believes happiness can be quantified, and a conversation between partygoers about where, literally, ‘the shit is going’. At times it is not unlike a drawing-room comedy, with its sharp wit, back-and-forth banter and clever insults.
The metafictional frame allows the novel to avoid the aftermath of its most dramatic events, dwelling instead on the act of remembering and reconstructing them. I’m not convinced this framing adds to the reader’s understanding of the narrator’s grief or the events being recounted. The narrator returns to remarkably similar emotional terrain at the end: melancholic and still lost, but perhaps slightly more hopeful for the future. For all its suspicion of the contemporary artworld and its machinations, The Floating World remains surprisingly sincere about art itself. This is especially persuasive when Eastham uses art to give shape to experiences that elude explanation – love, pregnancy, grief – reminding us that beneath the bullshit posturing of the artworld is an unexpectedly earnest faith that art can make felt what we cannot quite articulate.
The Floating World by Ben Eastham. Fitzcarraldo Editions , £14.99 (softcover)

articles.title_orig: Shaquille O'Neal addresses Fever's Kelsey Mitchell's remarks on Caitlin Clark, says to leverage the spotlight
articles.title_zh: Shaquille O'Neal addresses Fever's Kelsey Mitchell's remarks on Caitlin Clark, says to leverage the spotlight
articles.content_orig:
O'Neal tells OutKick that Mitchell, who recently talked about the extra attention Clark brings to the Fever, should leverage the spotlight to her advantage.
Shaquille O’Neal is no stranger to having a lot of eyeballs on him, both literally and figuratively. For Indiana Fever star Kelsey Mitchell, it’s been an adjustment.
During the Fever’s end-of-season press conference on Saturday, Mitchell said that with the attention Caitlin Clark draws, she and her teammates get a lot of flak for being on the same team as Clark. O’Neal, having played in large and small markets next to superstars like Kobe Bryant throughout his career and dealt with criticism from fans, said Mitchell should take advantage of the attention.
"My advice is to take advantage of all the eyes that are. If the eyes are on one person and you're next to that person, take advantage of them," O’Neal told OutKick in a recent interview.
This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE
Kelsey Mitchell #0 of the Indiana Fever drives to the basket against the Minnesota Lynx on Aug. 2, 2026, at Target Center in Minneapolis, Minn. (NBAE via Getty Images)
O’Neal reflected on his journey and the different markets he played in throughout his illustrious career.
"(I went to) a small high school, still being the No. 1 player in the country, starting off in a small market, eventually going to a big market, but then returning back to a small market and win another championship," O’Neal said.
Mitchell is a free agent at the end of the season and will be in high demand, as the 30-year-old has been an All-Star in each of the last four seasons and averaged a career-high 24.7 points per game this year. While Mitchell praised the organization, her comments drew speculation about whether she may leave the franchise with which she has spent the first nine seasons of her career.
O’Neal called Mitchell a "beautiful young lady and a fabulous young lady" and said he didn’t want to speak for her or about her to avoid breaking the athlete code, but he said he would advise her to stay in Clark’s orbit.
"I wish her well, but my advice if you're playing next to somebody that has eyes that can bring you extra income, make sure you always stay next to that person," O’Neal said.
Mitchell will enter free agency in late January, when the Fever will anxiously await her decision.
THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!
Shaquille O'Neal meets with fans at the CCC store in the Manufaktura shopping mall in Lodz, Poland, on Oct. 3, 2026. (Marcin Golba/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
No athlete, current or former, may brand himself or herself better than O’Neal. The Basketball Hall of Famer wanted to make sure he surrounded himself with the right people when he began his career.
"I would say the first thing you do, you have to surround yourself with people that are smarter than you," O’Neal said. "Fifty-two percent of all professional athletes went down and playing have nothing, so we maximized my potential. You know, learned a lot, did a lot, dreamed a lot, created a lot. I think in 1992, the way he marketed me and the way I marketed myself, a lot of a lot of athletes follow that even still to this day."
O’Neal’s renowned brand manager, Leonard Armato, told OutKick that the epitome of having a successful brand as an athlete is to not only promote oneself but also to make good business decisions. In today’s day and age, Armato said athletes can be their own media companies.
With social media being born during O’Neal’s career, Armato said that the four-time NBA champion was the first to embrace social media and that technology can amplify an athlete’s capabilities. For O’Neal, it was paramount that no matter what he did, he stay true to himself.
"But you always have to be true to yourself. You know, we went first time with Leonard, we had a meeting with the image consulting firm and they tried to create a different image and he stopped the guy in the meeting. He says, ‘I know you're an expert. I respect you what to do, but image is reality.’ So you definitely have to stay true to yourself," O’Neal said.
"A lot of people who form characters that they can't live up to. So, me for example, I am who I am. You know, my image is all about fun. I would love to be known as the ambassador of fun."

Kelsey Mitchell's WNBA salary jumped from under $60,000 to $1.4 million, but her press conference focused on the toll of playing with Caitlin Clark. (Getty Images)
While O’Neal’s brand is strong, he said he has made many mistakes. After making those mistakes, he leaned into his core values and stayed true to himself.
"Every time I fail, I try to memorize what I did wrong and just create a new program. But I don't like to say ‘You do this, you do this, you do that to each (mistake),’ but if you follow certain core values. To build relationships you have to stay true to yourself to learn from your failures and you have to do things the right in a consistent way, you could create a brand that will be known well beyond after your years of playing and you could be around forever," O’Neal said.
Armato said a key mistake athletes make is surrounding themselves with the wrong people. Armato has a book coming out in November called "MAXIMIZE," which details how to build and manage an athlete’s brand. O’Neal wrote the foreword to the book.

articles.title_orig: Cornell gang-rape accuser was 'misled' about criminal investigation, her lawyer says
articles.title_zh: Cornell gang-rape accuser was 'misled' about criminal investigation, her lawyer says
articles.content_orig:
One month ago, the woman now known to America as Cornell’s Jane Doe was living in New York City among thousands of other aspirational twentysomethings, attempting to break into the hotel industry and build a new life, according to her attorney, Thomas Giuffra.
But that plan has been derailed since she filed a lawsuit against Cornell University and others, alleging she was raped at a frat house in 2024.
Instead, Giuffra said, Doe spent Wednesday taping up paper to obscure the windows of her parents’ home out of fear that a gunman could attack her, and reeling from a swatting episode that he said prompted police to swarm their home Tuesday night with weapons drawn.
Doe is increasingly scared for her own safety, Giuffra said in a phone interview with CNN on Wednesday as he detailed his client’s deteriorating mental state after an escalating series of violent threats.
Officers pointed weapons at Jane Doe’s boyfriend, her brother and her father after receiving a bogus tip that “someone was killing people in the house” on Tuesday evening, he said.
Death threats, doxxing attempts and an outpouring of anger online have also been levied at his client, Giuffra added.
“I don’t think she’s in a good spot now,” Giuffra said. “She’s scared.”
The public fallout from her allegations have rocked one of the country’s leading educational institutions. The university, its campus police force and the Tompkins County District Attorney’s office have each faced scrutiny over how they initially investigated her claims. Anger among students was palpable during a Wednesday sit-in on the Ithaca, New York, campus.
Doe herself has been following media reports and social media posts on her case, Giuffra told CNN as he described a family reeling from a sudden and terrifying ordeal that punctured their sense of safety.
“Before (this week), it was just a lunatic fringe, which you can be dismissive of,” he said. “Now it’s somebody taking real steps to harm you, and that’s pretty frightening.”
At 7 p.m. on Tuesday evening, a police officer in Doe’s hometown was dispatched to respond to a disturbing call: A man had shot and killed his mother and then turned the gun on his sister.
The information was bogus. But the officer, believing an active-shooter situation was unfolding, rushed to Doe’s home, where he saw a car backing out from the driveway, according to a police report from the incident obtained by CNN.
As he apprehended the two men in the vehicle – later revealed to be Doe’s brother and her boyfriend – another figure emerged from the home’s doorway. “I’m the dad. What’s going on?” he yelled, according to the report. The man told police his daughter is Jane Doe of the Cornell case and that the family was “being threatened by numerous unknown people.”
The swatting incident was an escalation in a series of threats to Doe’s safety that have roiled her family this week. The term “swatting” refers to false tips made to law enforcement agencies with the intention of having armed officers deployed to somebody’s home or place of business.
“Luckily the brother was in his car, (he) put his hands up,” Giuffra told CNN on Wednesday, relaying the events of the night. “(Doe’s) boyfriend got thrown on the ground,” and her father also had “guns put in his face,” according to Giuffra. “If you had a trigger-happy cop, or somebody had done the wrong thing, somebody could have ended up dead,” he said.
Police are now investigating the swatting attempt, and the FBI is also looking into the events, according to Giuffra.
According to Doe’s lawyer and two police reports reviewed by CNN, police arrived moments after Doe received a separate phone call from somebody claiming to share a first name with one of the seven men she named in her civil complaint.
According to her account to officers in the reports, Doe “began panicking” when she received the call, “because (her phone) wouldn’t stop ringing.” She informed officers about that previous call while they were at her house following the swatting tip.
Before the night was over, Giuffra’s wife told him that she, too, had received a threatening phone call. “These people have done so much research into (Doe),” Giuffra said. It is not clear whether the separate threats cited in the police reports were connected.
Giuffra said he was in contact with Doe and her family on Wednesday. Her parents are angry and she is terrified, he said.
The lawyer shared with CNN an audio recording of a call he says was placed to his office on Wednesday afternoon. In the recording, a man identifies himself as “the person who called your client.”
The man also is heard saying: “I’m telling you guys simply, I think you should advise your client to withdraw the case. Otherwise blood will be shed.”
Tuesday’s swatting attack was an escalation of the potential dangers facing Doe since she filed her lawsuit last month, but it was far from the only threat she’s received, her lawyer said.
Giuffra estimated that dozens of threats have been made against her since mid-September, when his client filed a 101-page complaint alleging she had been sexually assaulted and raped by several members of the Xi chapter of Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity.
Doe’s civil suit was filed against the university, the fraternity, seven fraternity members and others. It alleges that members of the frat drugged and sexually assaulted her in October 2024 and invited other fraternity members in a group chat to join the assault. The suit also alleges the school failed to protect her and adequately punish the accused students, who all deny wrongdoing.
Giuffra detailed to CNN another threat: a text message, sent to Doe’s phone on Monday, with three emojis depicting guns.
Meanwhile, a handful of online personalities with large followings have led a campaign to uncover the identity of Doe, whose name was redacted in legal documents. One wrote on X to 347,000 followers in late September: “If you happen to know who this Cornell ‘Jane Doe’ is, get in touch and I would be happy to publish her name and identifying information.”
He later claimed to have identified her and said he shared that identity online before deleting his post. Such behavior is known as doxxing, or sharing someone’s personal information or identity online without their permission.
It has left Doe frightened and struggling to come to terms with the impact of the lawsuit, which has prompted outrage and scrutiny of how the university and its private police force initially investigated her claims.
On Wednesday, Doe was “taping paper over windows in the house she’s lived at her whole life,” Giuffra said, “so people can’t see into her house to take a shot at her.”
“I don’t get shook up very easily, but this shook me up. I didn’t want to have a body on my hands,” he said.
“The dad is … concerned for his daughter. He can’t believe this has happened out of something where she’s just trying to stand up for herself and be heard,” Giuffra added.
“But the parents are really strong people, and they’re going to protect their daughter.”
Doe had studied hotel administration at Cornell’s prestigious Nolan School of Hotel Administration, and it had been her “dream” to attend the school, Giuffra said. Her complaint says she traveled across the country and arrived at the school with the same “hopes, expectations and trepidations of other high school graduates.”
But she left the program without graduating after the alleged assault took place two years ago. Doe initially attempted to begin a career in New York City earlier this year, but after filing the lawsuit – “when everything hit the fan” – she instead returned to her family home, where she has been staying with her boyfriend, her lawyer said.
“The dream is lost,” Giuffra told CNN, referring to her hopes of working in the hospitality industry.
Instead, Doe has been hiding out at her parents’ home, where she has been following the intense media coverage of her case.

articles.title_orig: Amazon’s new Alexa Tablets are an iPad-inspired reboot, complete with the Play Store
articles.title_zh: Amazon’s new Alexa Tablets are an iPad-inspired reboot, complete with the Play Store
articles.content_orig:
Amazon has an all-new lineup of tablets ready to tempt you this holiday season, and for once, you might actually want to buy them. While the company has tried in previous years to make an upmarket play for relevancy in the tablet space, these new Alexa Tablets — RIP “Fire” — have the one thing everyone’s wanted for years: actual Play Store support.
Yes, a decade after ditching the “Kindle” branding in its tablet lineup, Amazon is ditching the Fire brand entirely for its new lineup of iPad competitors. That’s not me trying to write off its Android-powered rivals; rather, the sizes and designs all make for devices that, frankly, look like iPad knock-offs. Alexa Tablets come in three sizes: an 8-inch entry-level iPad Mini competitor, an 11-inch base iPad-esque slate, and a 12-inch “Pro” model that looks to be the most unique of the bunch. They’re all designed with aluminum bodies and, despite being much more expensive than the Fire tablets they’re replacing, still manage to undercut most of the market.
The 8.7-inch 60Hz Alexa Tablet 8 features 4GB of RAM, up to 128GB of storage, and comes in graphite, rosette, and teal, while the 90Hz 11-inch Alexa Tablet 11 features 8GB of RAM, up to 128GB of storage, and adds matcha and amethyst to the mix. Both run on a MediaTek 8189 8-core processor, a relatively recent chipset that appeared in a handful of seemingly-unreleased ChromeOS devices over the past year or so, before landing in these budget tablets. While I wouldn’t say there’s much to write home here about the specs — and again, the design is just absolutely a blatant copy of the iPad — it certainly sounds like a big upgrade over their predecessors.
And really, that comes down to the software. Despite Amazon’s current Android-less strategy on its Fire TV devices , the company seems to be doubling down on Android with its tablets. While it does have a unique launcher designed to push Alexa+, these things run proper Android, complete with the Play Store front and center on the device. YouTube is one of the highlighted apps on their store listings, and as someone who maintained Play Store sideloading guides at two different tech websites over the past decade, I can certainly say I never saw it coming. I have no idea how the actual software experience will feel day-to-day, but in terms of app support, it’s one problem that’s finally solved.
The star of the show, of course, is the 12-inch Alexa Tablet 12 Pro . This is, bar none, the most premium tablet Amazon has ever shipped, with a price that matches. It combines a 2.8K 3:2 120Hz display with quad speakers, 8GB of RAM, 128GB of storage, and a MediaTek Dimensity 8400 processor. That’s a real processor, and while I wouldn’t say it’s worthy of being called a flagship chipset, it’s undoubtedly the most powerful chip Amazon’s ever used. It’s a good sign when you’re using the same processor that a budget gaming-focused brand like Poco used just a year or two ago.
The 12-inch model also comes in an optional “nanomatte” version for an anti-glare experience, which also allows you to upgrade your RAM and storage to 16GB and 256GB, respectively. 16GB of RAM in an Amazon tablet — it’s a new day after all. And like its last attempt to go full-premium, the company does offer optional stylus and keyboard accessories for road warriors on a budget.
The Alexa Tablet 8 starts at $230 for the base 64GB model with lockscreen ads, or $250 without, while the Alexa Tablet 11 starts at $330 for its base model, or $350 for the ad-free version. Both feature a 128GB upgrade for $50 more. The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro starts at $500 for the base 128GB model; the nanomatte upgrade will run you $50 more. Meanwhile, that high-end 16/256 variant costs a whopping $680, and while that might sound pretty expensive on paper, it comes in well under Samsung’s latest 12-inch tablet for anyone who doesn’t need that level of processing power. Oh, and absolutely no ads on any of the 12 Pro models — the price you see is the price you pay, no upgrades necessary.

articles.title_orig: Odyssey Launches Odyssey-3, Its Most Powerful Foundation World Model Built to Power AI Across the Physical World
articles.title_zh: Odyssey Launches Odyssey-3, Its Most Powerful Foundation World Model Built to Power AI Across the Physical World
articles.content_orig:
Odyssey Launches Odyssey-3, Its Most Powerful Foundation World Model Built to Power AI Across the Physical World
New model demonstrates a shared understanding of the world across robots, humanoids, vehicles, drones, AI agents, and video games
Odyssey , an AI research company pioneering foundation world models, today announced Odyssey-3, its most powerful world model to date. The new model represents a significant advance toward general-purpose intelligence that can understand, predict, and interact with both physical and virtual environments.
This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261008756684/en/
Caption: Odyssey’s latest world model powering Flexion’s robot. Credit: Odyssey
World models learn from vast examples of the world evolving to predict and simulate what happens next, including how actions affect outcomes. Odyssey-3 gives intelligent systems a general understanding of how the world works before they are taught a specific task. The model has shown the ability to control robots and humanoids, drive vehicles, pilot drones, generate environments for training AI agents, and play video games. The new model has already been adopted by companies including Flexion, a leader in humanoid autonomy.
Trained on a vast dataset of visual observations of the world, Odyssey-3 builds on world models the company has been developing over the past three years. It has learned representations of physics, dynamics, cause and effect, and human behavior that can be applied across physical and virtual systems.
Using this pretrained foundation, Odyssey-3 enables physical agents: intelligent systems that can apply a shared understanding of the world across different machines, environments, and tasks. Rather than learning every new task entirely from scratch, these systems can draw on a broader model of how the world works and adapt that knowledge to new situations with relatively little additional experience.
“Odyssey-3 is a big step toward a single intelligence that can understand and operate in the world around us,” said Oliver Cameron, co-founder and CEO of Odyssey . “World models give physical agents a foundation of knowledge they can carry from one machine, environment, or task to another. We believe that the ability to learn broadly and then adapt with relatively little experience is the path toward increasingly general physical intelligence.”
The company has demonstrated Odyssey-3 across six domains:
Odyssey-3 is designed as a foundation that can span these domains rather than a model optimized for a single machine or application. By learning common representations of how environments behave and how actions change them, Odyssey is working toward world models that can transfer knowledge across increasingly diverse physical and virtual systems.
Odyssey is an AI lab pioneering general world models: causal, multimodal systems that learn to predict and interact with the world over long horizons. This foundational technology promises to revolutionize robotics, science, healthcare, education, gaming, defense, and beyond.
Odyssey’s founders previously pioneered one of the most complex applications of physical AI: self-driving cars. They’ve since brought together a world-class research team from DeepMind, Tesla, Waymo, Meta, Apple, and Wayve, whose members have contributed to language models, video models, world models and autonomous systems, including DeepMind Gemini, DeepMind Veo, Wayve GAIA and Tesla FSD.
Media: media@odyssey.systems

articles.title_orig: World Sight Day: Restoring sight where cataract surgery is scarce
articles.title_zh: World Sight Day: Restoring sight where cataract surgery is scarce
articles.content_orig:
Lloyd Williams, MD, PhD, discusses rising cataract blindness and low-cost surgery in conflict zones for World Sight Day.
Cataract remains a leading cause of vision impairment and blindness worldwide. At least 2.2 billion people have a near or distance vision impairment, and in at least 1 billion of those cases, the impairment could have been prevented or has yet to be addressed, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Cataract accounts for 94 million of those cases, and 1 in 2 people who need cataract surgery do not have access to it.¹
World Sight Day is an annual day of awareness held on the second Thursday of October and coordinated by the International Agency for the Prevention of Blindness (IAPB). This year, it falls on October 8. The 2026 #LoveYourEyes campaign centers on personal stories, lived experiences, and community action ahead of the first Global Summit for Eye Health on November 2 in Antigua and Barbuda.²
To mark the occasion, Lloyd Williams, MD, PhD , director of Duke Global Ophthalmology at Duke Eye Center in Durham, North Carolina, spoke with Ophthalmology Times about why cataract blindness continues to rise and how teams deliver high-quality surgery in low-resource settings. Williams received the American Academy of Ophthalmology's 2025 Outstanding Humanitarian Service Award for expanding access to cataract and corneal surgery in underserved regions.
Williams attributed the increase to aging populations in regions where ophthalmic care has not expanded, compounded by conflict and poverty that make many areas harder to reach. He cited a recent cataract camp in South Sudan.
"We literally had to negotiate a ceasefire in order to do cataract surgery," Williams told Ophthalmology Times .
Williams highlighted several organizations working to expand access to eye care. Readers can donate or get involved through the following: • Duke Global Ophthalmology: Give to Duke GO .³ • Cure Blindness Project: Donate ; ophthalmologists and practices can also join its Global Partners Program.⁴ • IAPB: Individuals can become a Love Your Eyes Visionary , and organizations can apply for membership .⁵ • CBM (Christian Blind Mission): Donate .⁶ • Sightsavers: Donate or fundraise through Sightsavers USA.⁷
On a recent trip to Abyei, surgery cost approximately $70 per case using manual small incision cataract surgery (MSICS), which requires a microscope as the only electrical equipment. In skilled hands, Williams said, MSICS achieves results roughly equivalent to those in the US. A $700,000 donation this year is expected to fund approximately 9000 surgeries, a volume he said would not be possible with phacoemulsification or laser-based approaches.
"I strongly believe that we're not providing somebody substandard care," Williams said.
Williams also addressed studies linking cataract surgery to lower rates of dementia diagnosis, which cannot yet establish cause and effect. He recalled veterans whose anxiety and depression appeared to improve after surgery during his residency, and he said he discusses the cognitive benefits of sight with families of older patients. Reflecting on his own vision problem as a resident, he described sight as "something that you could lose just like your arm."

articles.title_orig: Webinar will commemorate World Food Day with theme “Innovate today. Nourish tomorrow”
articles.title_zh: Webinar will commemorate World Food Day with theme “Innovate today. Nourish tomorrow”
articles.content_orig:
A webinar on 16 October will commemorate World Food Day and say farewell to the UN special rapporteur for the Right to Water and Sanitation.
The webinar will take the World Food Day theme “ Innovate today. Nourish tomorrow.” The discussion will explore what innovation can look like when we place food security, water, land, human rights, and ecological sustainability at the centre.
World Food Day is observed on 16 October each year and provides an opportunity to draw attention to hunger and food insecurity while strengthening collective action towards food systems that are sustainable, equitable, and resilient. This year ’ s webinar will bring together United Nations mandate holders, faith-based organisations, civil society organisations, and community practitioners to explore some of the challenges shaping food insecurity today – including poverty, unsustainable agricultural practices and climate change – and to share approaches that are contributing to resilience, food sovereignty, and sustainable livelihoods.
The session will also provide an opportunity to hear from Prof. Pedro Arrojo-Agudo, UN special rapporteur on the human right to safe drinking water and sanitation, whose six-year mandate concludes in November 2026.

articles.title_orig: New GETI publication explores future of Christian unity
articles.title_zh: New GETI publication explores future of Christian unity
articles.content_orig:
A new publication from the World Council of Churches (WCC) Commission on Ecumenical Education and Formation (EEF) brings together the voices and theological reflections of young ecumenists from around the world who attended the 2025 edition of the WCC Global Ecumenical Theological Institute (GETI). It brings fresh inputs to the pressing question for the churches today: Where now for visible unity?
From left: Rev. Prof. Dr Meehyun Chung, moderator of the WCC Commission on Ecumenical Education and Formation; Prof. Dr Ani Ghazaryan Drissi, WCC programme executive for Ecumenical Theological Education and coordinator of GETI 2025; Rev. Dr Nathan Digby, GETI 2025 facilitator and member of the WCC Commission on Ecumenical Education and Formation; during the launch event of the GETI 2025 book on 8 October.
“ GETI 2025: Voices and Visions of Transformative Unity,” edited by Prof. Dr Ani Ghazaryan Drissi and Rev. Prof. Teddy Chalwe Sakupapa, emerges from the WCC ’ s 4th GETI, held in the context of the Sixth World Conference on Faith and Order in Wadi El Natrun, Egypt. The publication, launched on 8 October, during the biannual meeting of the EEF Commission, comes at a significant moment.
“ The fruits of ecumenical dialogue must take root in the lives of our churches,” said Ghazaryan. “ The GETI 2025 message brought this bold challenge to the Sixth World Conference on Faith and Order and the wider ecumenical movement: let the unity we confess become the life we share.”
This publication carries that call forward, she added, through voices and visions rooted in different churches, cultures, and lived realities. “ Their theological reflections invite us to ask how the fruits of ecumenical dialogue can shape our communities, deepen our relationships, and renew our common witness,” said Ghazaryan. “ They call us to listen more deeply, confront exclusion, and share responsibility for the future of our churches.”
Bossey students who took part of GETI 2025 shared their testimonies during the launch event.
The volume presents a global and contextually grounded exploration of Christian unity. Its contributors reflect on reception, Nicaea, pilgrimage, trust and companionship, while also addressing colonial wounds, trauma, migration, ethnic violence, Palestine, digital ecumenism, and ecological crisis.
Rather than treating unity as an abstract theological ideal, the book emphasizes unity as something that must be embodied through relationships, truth-telling, healing, solidarity, and public witness. Its concluding message describes young ecumenists as contributors to the present and future of the ecumenical movement.
GETI 2025 facilitator and EEF commissioner Rev. Dr Nathan Digby explained that a central goal of the WCC ’ s Ecumenical Theological Education work is to provide opportunities for emerging ecumenical leaders to be formed in ecumenism and to ensure that their voices are heard, encouraged, and shared with the wider church.
“ The publication of GETI 2025: Voices and Visions for Transformative Unity gives concrete expression to this commitment,” he said. “ As part of their theological formation, students participating in GETI 2025 developed academic papers exploring the theme of visible Christian unity in relation to their own theological interests, contexts, and experiences.”
This volume recognizes and celebrates their intellectual and theological work while creating a platform through which their perspectives can contribute to broader conversations about the future of Christian unity, added Digby.
“ By bringing these emerging voices together in one publication, GETI 2025: Voices and Visions for Transformative Unity not only documents an important dimension of the GETI experience but also invests in the next generation of ecumenical thinkers and leaders, whose insights and visions are essential for shaping a more transformative and visible unity among Christians.”
Published by WCC Publications, the book offers churches, theological institutions, students, and ecumenical partners a rich resource for reflection and conversation on the future of Christian unity.
The session also included the presentation of the GETI Visual Report and a short video featuring voices and moments of GETI 2025.
The EEF Commission is meeting at the WCC Ecumenical Institute at Bossey 4-9 October.

articles.title_orig: FDA-approved epilepsy drug may help reverse osteoarthritis damage
articles.title_zh: FDA-approved epilepsy drug may help reverse osteoarthritis damage
articles.content_orig:
For millions of people with osteoarthritis, pain and stiffness can make everyday activities increasingly difficult. Common treatments, including over-the-counter medications and steroid injections, may reduce symptoms for a time, but they do not prevent the underlying joint damage from progressing.
New research from Yale suggests a different approach. In a study published in Bioactive Materials , scientists found that the medication lacosamide can serve two purposes in osteoarthritis, reducing joint pain while also reversing cartilage damage. The effects were particularly strong when the drug was delivered directly into the joint using a specialized hydrogel.
Why osteoarthritis damages cartilage
Osteoarthritis is often called a condition caused by wear and tear, but that description leaves out much of the biology involved.
Within a healthy joint, cells known as chondrocytes help maintain cartilage by continuously balancing the creation of new tissue with the removal of old material. Osteoarthritis disrupts that balance. Cartilage begins to break down faster than it can be replaced, eventually allowing bones to rub against one another. As the disease advances, some patients may ultimately require joint reconstruction procedures such as a total knee replacement.
"There is a major unmet need in osteoarthritis," says the study's principal investigator and Charles W. Ohse Professor of Orthopaedics & Rehabilitation, Chuan-Ju Liu, PhD. "We need therapies that don't just mask pain but actually change how the disease progresses."
At present, no medicine approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration can both stop osteoarthritis pain and prevent the structural breakdown of cartilage. The work led by Liu suggests that it may be possible to address both problems with a single therapeutic strategy.
The researchers repurposed an existing medication and paired it with an advanced gel designed to keep the drug inside the joint. The approach could potentially preserve joint tissue while delivering sustained pain relief without relying on addictive opioids.
A protein linked to pain and cartilage loss
The research focuses on Nav1.7, a protein that functions as a sodium channel. These channels act as microscopic gates in cell membranes and play an important role in electrical signaling.
Nav1.7 was long thought to operate primarily in specialized nerve cells that transmit pain signals to the brain. More recent work from Liu and his team, however, revealed that the protein is also highly active in chondrocytes, the cells responsible for maintaining cartilage.
Nav1.7 is relatively quiet in healthy joints. In osteoarthritis, however, its activity increases substantially. The researchers found that this heightened activity can intensify pain signaling while also pushing chondrocytes toward breaking down the cartilage they would normally help preserve.
That makes Nav1.7 an unusual therapeutic target because it appears to influence both the sensation of pain and the physical deterioration of joint tissue.
"When Nav1.7 becomes dysregulated, it contributes to both joint degeneration and pain," Liu says. "Our findings suggest that Nav1.7 is a dual-acting target. By blocking this single protein, we can potentially quiet the pain nerves and tell the cartilage cells to not only stop breaking down but start repairing as well."
Epilepsy drug shows potential for cartilage repair
Instead of creating an entirely new medication, Liu's team tested drugs that already inhibit sodium channels. Among them, lacosamide produced strong biological effects at considerably lower concentrations and offered a better safety profile than older drugs in the same class.
Lacosamide is already used as a treatment for epilepsy, but the researchers found that its effects on cartilage depended heavily on the dose.
More was not necessarily better. At an ideal low concentration, lacosamide encouraged cells to produce proteins involved in building cartilage while also suppressing processes that break tissue down. When the concentration was either too high or too low, those benefits began to fade.
"This tells us the system is finely tuned," Liu notes. "There is an optimal range where the drug helps restore balance without overcorrecting. What stood out was not just its effectiveness, but how little of a dose was needed."
Further investigation revealed that lacosamide also changes the way cells communicate. The drug stimulated the release of two beneficial signaling proteins, HSP70 and midkine.
HSP70 helps cells respond to stress and supports tissue repair, while midkine helps regulate inflammation and protect joint tissue from degeneration. Together, the proteins appear to create conditions that are more favorable for maintaining cartilage.
"These proteins create a supportive environment for cartilage maintenance," Liu explains. "They allow the effects of the drug to extend beyond individual cells and influence the entire tissue."
Smart hydrogel keeps the drug inside the joint
Oral treatment with lacosamide was effective in preclinical testing, but drugs taken by mouth circulate throughout the body, increasing the potential for unwanted effects elsewhere.
The researchers therefore investigated intra-articular injection, which allows the medication to be placed directly inside the affected joint.
There was still a significant problem to overcome. "The knee joint, which is also the most common location for osteoarthritis, naturally acts like a leaky bucket," Liu says. "The body's drainage system can clear out liquids injected into the knee within hours."
To keep the medication in place longer, the team created a specialized hydrogel made from Collagen II. The material responds to temperature. It remains liquid while inside a cool syringe, then becomes a firm, jelly-like material after reaching body temperature.
Once inside the joint, the gel acts as a storage site for lacosamide, keeping the medication concentrated in the affected area while gradually releasing it over several weeks.
"The hydrogel acts as a local reservoir," Liu says. "It holds the drug in place in the location it is needed most and releases it slowly over time. It transforms a daily pill into a long-lasting, local treatment that stays active for a month or longer."
In the same preclinical studies, one injection of the lacosamide-containing gel every four weeks prevented cartilage loss more effectively than taking an oral dose every day.
Existing drug could speed clinical testing
One important advantage of lacosamide is that the medication is already approved for use in people. That could make it possible to move toward clinical studies in osteoarthritis patients more quickly than would be possible with a completely new drug.
Lacosamide has also been tested in humans with certain nerve-related pain conditions caused by Nav1.7 mutations. Those results give the researchers greater confidence that the effects seen in laboratory studies could eventually translate into meaningful pain relief for patients.
The work also reflects a broader direction in medicine that combines drugs with advanced biomaterials to control exactly where and how treatments are delivered. If the approach proves successful in people, it could eventually reduce the number of procedures patients need, limit unwanted side effects, and provide longer-lasting protection against structural joint damage.
"We are not just developing a treatment," Liu concludes. "We are developing a system that allows the medicine to work more effectively where it matters most. Our goal is to move beyond symptom control and towards true disease modification. This effort brings us closer to that reality."

articles.title_orig: For Mamdani, Oct. 7 Anniversary Sets Off Anger and Bitterness
articles.title_zh: For Mamdani, Oct. 7 Anniversary Sets Off Anger and Bitterness
articles.content_orig:
New York’s mayor marked the third anniversary of Hamas’ October 7 attacks on Israel on Wednesday with a statement that has sparked backlash among some Jewish leaders.
In his statement, Mayor Zohran Mamdani acknowledged the “horrific war crimes of October 7” while also accusing Israel of committing war crimes and genocide in Gaza.
The mayor was met with boos as he arrived at a vigil in remembrance of October 7 on Wednesday night in Union Square, video from CNN affiliate WABC showed . Later, he attended a meeting with Palestinian New Yorkers.
“This day is profoundly painful for so many New Yorkers. It marks three years since the horrific war crimes of October 7. On that day, Hamas killed more than 1,100 Israelis and abducted 251 others. We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss,” Mamdani wrote in his statement.
“The suffering did not begin nor end that day,” the statement continued. “It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza, in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians —including more than 21,000 children. Even since the so-called ceasefire, more than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed. That suffering has intensified with every Israeli bomb dropped on ambulances waiting outside hospitals, every drone strike targeting a residential building or journalist, and every shipment of food aid turned away at a border crossing. Many New Yorkers are reckoning with this unbearable grief, and we mourn alongside them —all while knowing that our tax dollars fund these war crimes,” Mamdani wrote.
“Three years later, we must refuse to accept a world in which occupation and apartheid continue, where war crimes are met with impunity, and our federal government continues its complicity with every arms shipment. To honor the dead, we must fight for a world in which every person can live with freedom, safety, and dignity,” the statement finished.
Hamas-led gunmen stormed Israeli communities along the border with Gaza on October 7 , 2023, killing more than 1,200 people, including children, women and elderly people. The attackers also took 251 hostages.
The mayor, a prominent critic of Israel’s government, received immediate backlash from some Jewish leaders on social media for his statement.
Jonathan Greenblatt, the CEO of the Anti-Defamation League, accused Mamdani of “weaponizing a day meant for mourning the worst massacre of Jews since the Holocaust to recycle your usual antizionist talking points,” in a post on X.
“The city with the largest Jewish population outside Israel deserves a mayor who can honor the dead without exploiting them,” he wrote. The Anti-Defamation League has launched a “Mamdani Monitor” to track the mayor’s administration.
CNN’s Christiane Amanpour interviews Mayor Zohran Mamdani
The president and director of the Auschwitz Jewish Center Foundation similarly referred to New York’s status as the city with the largest Jewish community outside Israel, saying “the Jewish people should be afforded this one day to mourn the murdered, the raped and the children left orphaned, without having their grief reframed as an indictment of Israel.”
“Palestinians have suffered enormously from the war Hamas unleashed, and their suffering deserves recognition,” Jack Simony wrote, adding Mamdani “should understand the weight of this day for the Jewish New Yorkers he represents.”
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee called Mamdani’s statement a “disgraceful moral failure.” Mamdani has denounced the organization for its spending in US elections.
The mayor responded to criticism at a news conference Thursday.
“I was proud to attend last night’s vigil, as I did last year, to listen to testimonies from family members of those who were killed on October 7, and those who’ve been killed in the three years since, and all of whom united in a vision for peace and an end to the genocide in Gaza,” the mayor said. He added, “As for those protesting me, I am the mayor of New York City, and this is what I signed up for.”
He reiterated his belief that the Israeli government has used the October 7 attack as a “justification for an ongoing genocide against Palestinians.”
“There must be room to reckon with the ways in which so many New Yorkers’ lives have been shattered, and that, to me, is a part of what it means to believe in a sense of humanity — that we need not choose between which death we will mourn and which we will ignore; that we can reckon with the fact that all of it is to be opposed,” he said.
But the mayor’s position has appeared to create divisions even within his own administration and City Council. On Wednesday, Julie Menin, the speaker of the New York City Council, called for the creation of the city’s first permanent October 7 memorial.
She left Thursday’s news conference before the mayor took questions. Asked if he planned to approve the creation of such a memorial, Mamdani said his administration is reviewing the proposal.
Last month, the mayor announced the first-ever municipal strategy for New York City to combat antisemitism, including tens of millions of dollars in funding for hate crime prevention and Jewish cultural centers.
Mamdani unveils strategy to combat antisemitism in New York City
Mamdani, who has faced accusations of antisemitism from some Jewish groups over his criticisms of Israel and his handling of protests outside synagogues, has attempted to make outreach to Jewish communities in the city a strong element of his administration.
During his campaign, he suggested as mayor he would seek to arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu under an International Criminal Court warrant for war crimes, even though the US is not a signatory to the ICC. The mayor acknowledged earlier this summer that he would not have the legal authority to do so.

articles.title_orig: A Rare Image of Mars at Dawn Reveals the Beauty of Its Ancient Cliffs
articles.title_zh: A Rare Image of Mars at Dawn Reveals the Beauty of Its Ancient Cliffs
articles.content_orig:
The captivating shapes of wind-carved crags called yardangs are revealed in this zoomed-in crop of a broader panorama captured by NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover on Aug. 11, 2026. Scientists are eager to learn more about how the yardang layer formed.
Sunlight illuminates wind-carved cliffs in a dramatic new image.
A newly released panorama captured by NASA’s Curiosity rover offers the most detailed view yet of distant, wind-carved Martian cliffs, highlighting features the mission’s scientists have long been waiting to see up close. The scene was snapped at 8:30 a.m. local Mars time, showing striking blue hues in the foreground as bright morning light illuminates crags known as yardangs on the horizon.
The panorama was captured by Curiosity’s Mastcam on Aug. 11, the 4,982nd Martian day, or sol, of the mission, and comprises six individual images that were stitched together after being sent to Earth. Unlike most of Curiosity’s Mastcam images, this one was processed without white balancing, preserving the early morning appearance.
The six shots that make up this panorama, captured by NASA’s Curiosity on Aug. 11, were stitched together after being sent back to Earth. Unlike most images from the rover’s Mastcam, this one was processed without the usual white balancing — an artistic choice that preserves the early morning appearance.
The yardang layer extends roughly 10 miles (16 kilometers) across the northwestern reaches of Mount Sharp, a 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain that Curiosity has been ascending since 2014. In fact, the rover recently passed another milestone in its ascent, reaching 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) of elevation — the most ever climbed on Mars. As it draws ever-closer to the yardangs, mission scientists expect to get even more amazing imagery — and, they hope, answers to how these cliffs were created.
Mount Sharp is made up of layers, each recording a distinct period of Mars’ history. By studying them, scientists have been able to learn more about lakes and streams that covered this part of the Red Planet billions of years ago. Eventually, the water dried up and left salty minerals behind. After new material stopped settling on the mountain, some of it may have been stripped away by wind, giving rise to the yardangs.
This artist’s concept shows Mount Sharp, the 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain that NASA’s Curiosity has been ascending since 2014. The location of the yardang layer, which the rover recently captured from a distance, is indicated by an ellipse annotation on the mountain’s northwestern shoulder.
NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover captured this view looking back at the floor of Gale Crater on Sept. 5, 2026. Just nine days prior, the rover had marked 1 kilometer of elevation gain above the crater floor since beginning its ascent of Mount Sharp in 2014.
“The yardang layer looks out of place. It’s the wrong color, the layers tilt at an odd angle, and it almost appears plastered on,” said Ashwin Vasavada, Curiosity project scientist of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “But that’s what makes it exciting to reach. No one is sure exactly what created this layer, but one idea is it may be ash deposited by ancient volcanic eruptions.”
Curiosity is in the second year of its fifth extended mission, which started with an exploration of the spiderweb-like boxwork ridges . The rover will spend most of the next year or so driving through layers enriched with sulfates and carbonates, both signs of ancient drying on the surface. Sometime in 2027, scientists hope to reach the base of the yardangs, where Curiosity will be able to use its robotic arm to collect one-of-a-kind data on these mysterious features.
From Mars to the Milky Way — never miss a discovery! Delivered straight to your inbox.
Curiosity was built by NASA JPL, which is managed by Caltech in Pasadena, California. NASA JPL leads the mission on behalf of the agency’s Science Mission Directorate in Washington as part of its Mars Exploration Program portfolio. Malin Space Science Systems in San Diego built and operates Mastcam.

articles.title_orig: Donald Trump’s Texas rally rocked by repeated protests
articles.title_zh: Donald Trump’s Texas rally rocked by repeated protests
articles.content_orig:
Trump briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage
Send us your questions on how the US economy is shaping the midterm elections
Donald Trump’s latest campaign rally was rocked by repeated protests on Wednesday as the US president urged Texas voters to back the embattled Senate candidate Ken Paxton.
At least half a dozen demonstrators interrupted the US president during his remarks in San Antonio, with some led away by police. One was physically assaulted by an older Trump supporter as he tried to leave the arena.
Trump briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage. “He’s going back home to mom,” the president said after the man was removed. “But what he doesn’t know is his mom voted for Trump.”
Supporters waving cowboy hats and chanting “USA” drowned out some of the protesters, while Trump told demonstrators to “get the hell out of here”. He mocked their appearance and claimed without evidence that “they’re paid by enemies of our nation”.
The president also used Wednesday’s rally to address recent comments in which he appeared to suggest that Iran could destroy Los Angeles or San Diego, earning widespread condemnation from Democrats.
In remarks that were again less than crystal clear, Trump said: “I said it the other day, let them hit a missile into San Diego or Los Angeles on the way. Let them hit – you want to see a horror show? You want to see problems? Let them hit San Diego. Let them hit Los Angeles and you want to see some bad things happen.
“You want to see a country that would be in freefall. We’re not going to let that happen. We protect our cities, we protect our country, we’re not letting that happen. And they’d use it, too. They’d use it.”
Trump was making his third trip to Texas in less than a month as Republicans pour money into races they had expected to win comfortably in November’s midterm elections.
Paxton, whom Trump endorsed during the Republican primary after turning against the incumbent senator John Cornyn, was called on stage by the president and thanked him for his support.
“Mr President, I want to thank you for coming for me, for coming for us, and for coming for Texas,” Paxton said. “We are going to win this race.”
Trump described Paxton as “perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America”, and said: “He was tough and he was with us all the way. He’s a fantastic man.”
The Republican campaign to maintain control of the Senate has become increasingly focused on Texas, where Democrat James Talarico has emerged as a serious threat. A New York Times/Siena College poll released last weekend showed Talarico leading Paxton 51% to 45% among likely voters. Texas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988.
Trump won the state by almost 14 percentage points in 2024, but his approval rating has fallen sharply. A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday put his approval rating at 32%, while registered voters preferred Democrats to Republicans 44%-37%.
after newsletter promotion
Trump’s relationship with Paxton has sometimes appeared uneasy. Trump called Paxton “a pain in the ass sometimes” last week, but on Wednesday did not discuss a leaked recording of Paxton in which the Senate candidate reportedly complained about the war in Iran, rising fuel prices and the way his campaign was being run.
Instead he spent much of the rally attacking Talarico, whom he repeatedly referred to as “Tala-freako”. He claimed without evidence that Talarico is vegan and recently disappeared: “He’s sick because he’s been forced to eat meat for political reasons and he’s throwing up all over the place.”
Trump insisted: “The people of Texas are not going to let weak, gutless, self-hating, transgender-promoting freak shows destroy everything that we’ve built.”
The president’s political difficulties in Texas were underlined by the absence of the Republican governor, Greg Abbott, a close Trump ally who is himself facing a competitive re-election race against the Democratic state representative Gina Hinojosa.
Abbott was instead due to attend the dedication of a hospital about 330 miles away. Democrats seized on his decision not to appear with Trump.
Republicans have now devoted more than $300m to elections in Texas, according to the Associated Press, while Trump’s broader 32-day campaign blitz has taken him through several Republican-leaning states, including Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska.

articles.title_orig: Amoris laetitia: Pastoral experiences in Asia and challenges of digital world
articles.title_zh: Amoris laetitia: Pastoral experiences in Asia and challenges of digital world
articles.content_orig:
Families today are âa challenging mosaic of diverse realities, marked by joys, hopes, struggles and wounds. The family is not only a place to which the Church brings the Gospel. It is also a place from which the Gospel comes alive â from one generation to another, from one family to another, and from families to society.â
Cardinal Filipe Neri Ferrão, Metropolitan Archbishop of Goa and Daman, opened his address with this reflection at the start of the second day of Pope Leo XIVâs meeting with the heads of the Eastern Churches and the presidents of the Bishopsâ Conferences, ten years after Amoris laetitia .
The Indian Cardinal addressed the theme âFamilies today: reality, beauty and challenges. Discerning the signs of the times through the experience of families and the Churchâs pastoral commitment today.â
He invited participants in the meeting, conducted in a synodal style, to ask themselves in their discernment: âWhat is the Holy Spirit asking the Church to change?â
This concerned ânot only in what we do for the families, but in how we understand, accompany and empower them as protagonists of the Gospel and as enduring loci of Godâs revelation.â
Drawing on his experience as a pastor in Asia, particularly in India, Cardinal Neri Ferrão acknowledged that families had changed in their identity, nature, and composition, with smaller households, new forms of cohabitation, and interreligious marriages.
Families were increasingly on the move, and many faced economic insecurity, poverty, unemployment, and uncertainty about the future.
âChristian families in many parts of India and Asia,â the Cardinal stressed, âmust also live amid growing religious polarisation and hostility, making the public expression and transmission of faith increasingly difficult.â
Yet, these families also offered the Church beauty through their care for children, the elderly, the sick, and vulnerable people. Even amid poverty and uncertainty, the Cardinal explained, âour families continue to create positive spaces for joy and hope.â
Following the publication of Amoris laetitia , he recalled, the Churches in India and across Asia âlistened first to families,â and that listening âshaped how we walk with them. We now see marriage preparation as the start of a lifelong journey, offer spiritual renewal and counselling to couples and children, and keep forming families and lay leaders over time.â
He stressed that pastoral ministry needed to move âfrom mission to families to mission among families.â Families were not simply recipients of assistance but, in his words, âthe Church's partners in mission.â
Cardinal Neri Ferrão concluded by recounting the experience of a priest who had begun family ministry in his parish not with a program, but by visiting a family experiencing underlying difficulties in communication between the parents and between them and their children. It had begun with âa conversation and a willingness to listen.â
The second speaker, Vincenzo Rosito, Professor of the History and Culture of Family Institutions at the Pontifical Lateran University and Vice Dean of the Pontifical John Paul II Theological Institute for Marriage and Family Sciences, summed up his address with questions to guide participantsâ synodal discernment.
He began with an invitation inspired by Pope Leo XIVâs reflections in the encyclical Magnifica humanitas : âLet each of us be mindful of the relationships we build within our own families and within the Church.â
Professor Rosito stressed that âfamily practices, in fact, help us to understand how churches and families learn from one another. Both the Church and the family, in fact, learn through the practices of their daily lives.â
He then offered a question for participants to consider as a father, mother, theologian, or pastor: âAm I able to recognise and share with others at least one new thing that I have learnt to do, or to do differently, in recent years of my family or pastoral life?â
Changes in family life, Prof. Rosito explained, âare not problemsâ but âhuman activities.â Recalling Amoris laetitia , he presented them as an opportunity, as concrete processes âin which individuals and families act, react, learn and develop new resources.â
âConsider, for example,â the political philosopher continued, âhow the use of new digital technologies is transforming the daily habits of families and the way children are brought up.â
The family and the Church, Prof. Rosito continued, âlearn together through change.â He drew on the Gospel image of Jesus, Joseph, and Maryâs flight into Egypt.
He noted that today, âdrawing on the experiences of refugee and migrant families, some Christian communities are re-establishing themselves as ârefuge churchesââ for those arriving in a new land or making a long journey.
He also addressed the tragedy of violence shared by many families: âThe insecurity stemming from social and political violence is a worrying reality that many Churches must deal with today, in their daily lives.â Such insecurity, he warned, could âeven devour family bonds and church relationships themselves.â
Josephâs dream was also part of the experience of this flight.
âTo dream, to imagine new forms for the Church,â Prof. Rosito concluded, âalso means renewing what we already do. To imagine the Church means being willing to learn from one another, whilst we are transformed together, as churches and as families.â
His final question for discernment was therefore: âWhat do we need, amidst the light and shadow of today, to learn and imagine new ways of being a family and new ways of being the Church?â
