articles.title_orig: Texts Show Kimberly Guilfoyle Seeking $100,000 and Offering Access to Trump Officials
articles.title_zh: Texts Show Kimberly Guilfoyle Seeking $100,000 and Offering Access to Trump Officials
articles.content_orig:
Natasha previously reported on features, and UK news and politics. She became a full-time features writer in 2025, later joining the Washington bureau in 2026. She can be found on Instagram @natasha_leake
Donald Trump Jr’s former fiancée allegedly put pressure on a donor and supporter of Donald Trump to pay her $100,000 (£75,000) American Express bill.
Kimberly Guilfoyle, now the US ambassador to Greece , had promised Eric Deters, a congressional Republican candidate for Kentucky, access to administration officials in exchange for up to $1m (£750,000), the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported.
According to the newspaper, Mr Deters was hopeful that the new Trump administration would intervene in his personal tax and legal issues.
Ms Guilfoyle, 56, had apparently offered to use her influence within the White House to help Mr Deters. The WSJ reported that she had forwarded him messages she sent to the head of the Internal Revenue Service about his situation, and had kept him up-to-date on her efforts to lobby the US justice department.
She also told him she needed her $100,000 American Express bill paid off before the Senate confirmation hearing for her ambassadorship, which was set to take place in July 2025, the newspaper reported.
“Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” she allegedly texted Mr Deters on Signal, according to messages reviewed by the Wall Street Journal.
“It won’t show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express,” she allegedly wrote, adding: “please”.
Mr Deters told the outlet that Ms Guilfoyle promised him, “I will be your Trump ride or die, forever and ever,” if he came up with the money. But “she never came through on anything”.
Mr Deters never made the credit card payment, telling Ms Guilfoyle it would cost him his marriage, the WSJ reported.
Ms Guilfoyle has been contacted for comment by The Telegraph.
A lawyer for Ms Guilfoyle told the WSJ that the ambassador disputed the authenticity of the messages.
He added that she had been paid to speak at events after her nomination and that she “was owed a balance for travelling to and supporting these patriotic events”.
A US embassy official told the Wall Street Journal: “Guilfoyle’s career in and out of public service is guided by deep and abiding values. She was fully vetted by the bipartisan Senate Foreign Relations committee and confirmed by the US Senate.
“The ambassador remains committed to representing the American people with dedication and integrity.”
Last week, Democrats called for an inquiry into Ms Guilfoyle, urging the state department to review her conduct after it was revealed that she promoted a Greek company whose lobbyist travelled with her to meetings with governments across the Balkans.

articles.title_zh: Northern lights possible across the US this weekend as 3 CMEs head for Earth
articles.content_orig:
Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.
By submitting your information, you confirm you are aged 16 or over,
have read our Privacy Policy and agree to the Terms & Conditions . Geographical rules apply.

Three solar eruptions are heading toward Earth and could give the northern lights a serious boost across parts of the U.S. this weekend.
The incoming coronal mass ejections ( CMEs ) — vast clouds of plasma and magnetic field from the sun — erupted from sunspot region AR4549 on Oct. 6 and Oct. 7. They're currently hurtling toward Earth and could arrive in relatively quick succession. This is great news for aurora chasers.
NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) forecasts the most significant CME to reach Earth on Oct. 9, with the second potentially delivering a glancing blow around the same time. But that's not all. A third CME erupted on Oct. 8 and could arrive around Oct. 10-11.
NOAA's aurora forecast suggests auroral activity could be enhanced across northern North America. Exactly how far south the aurora might appear remains uncertain and depends on how the incoming CMEs interact with Earth's magnetic field .
G2 geomagnetic storm conditions are forecast for Oct. 9 and during such storms, auroras have previously been observed as far south as New York and Idaho .
While northern U.S. states currently have the best prospects, skywatchers farther south shouldn't completely write off their chances just yet. With multiple CMEs approaching Earth in quick succession, there's still considerable uncertainty over how geomagnetic conditions will develop. If the incoming eruptions interact favorably with Earth's magnetic field, auroras could potentially reach much farther south than currently anticipated.
So if you're at mid-latitudes, make sure those aurora alerts are switched on and your camera batteries are charged. This could be an interesting few days for northern lights enthusiasts!
For real-time forecasts based on your location, consider using a space weather app. A great option is "My Aurora Forecast & Alerts" (available for iOS and Android ). For a deeper dive into space weather conditions, "Space Weather Live" is another excellent choice (available for iOS and Android )
NOAA's latest 3-day forecast gives us an approximate idea of when geomagnetic activity (and hopefully aurora activity) could pick up.
Forecasters currently predict minor (G1) conditions between 11 p.m.–2 a.m. EDT on Oct. 8–9 (03:00 and 06:00 GMT on Oct. 9), followed by a possible G2 (Moderate) peak between 5–8 a.m. EDT (0900-1200) on Oct. 9.
But don't set your alarm just yet — these timings are far from set in stone.
With multiple CMEs potentially reaching Earth in quick succession, forecasting exactly when the geomagnetic activity will intensify if particularly challenging. So don't limit your northern lights hunt to those forecast windows. And don't write off the rest of the weekend.
Another CME could deliver a glancing blow late on Oct. 10 or early Oct 11, potentially bringing further geomagnetic activity and yet another opportunity to catch the northern lights.
This is where things get complicated.
Current modelling places the arrival of the main Oct. 6 CME in the early hours of Oct. 9 (UTC), although forecasts carry an uncertainty of several hours. Space weather physicist Tamitha Skov notes that the two Oct. 6 CMEs could reach Earth in relatively quick succession, delivering a one-two punch to Earth's magnetic field. However, their journey may be influenced by the surrounding solar wind , making precise arrival times difficult to pin down.
The third CME could follow late Oct. 11 or early Oct. 11 (UTC), potentially prolonging unsettled geomagnetic activity and aurora prospects into the weekend. And remember, even an Earth-directed CME doesn't guarantee a spectacular aurora display. Much will depend on how the magnetic fields carried by these eruptions interact with Earth's magnetic field when they arrive.
With AR4549 still magnetically complex and facing Earth, more solar activity could be on the way. The sun sure is keeping us on our toes this week!
Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.
Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.
She will be a guest speaker aboard HX's Solar Eclipse Expedition in August 2026 and will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

articles.title_orig: A hurricane could cripple US refining when the world can least afford it
articles.title_zh: A hurricane could cripple US refining when the world can least afford it
articles.content_orig:
The global energy system is already being pushed to the brink. A hurricane barreling down on America’s refining nerve center is the last thing that’s needed.
Isaias, the Atlantic season’s first hurricane , is arriving at a time when there is almost no margin for error.
US refineries, mostly located along the Gulf Coast, are running as hard as they can to offset war-driven outages overseas. Fuel inventories that act as shock absorbers have already been tapped. And America’s emergency oil stockpile is at the lowest level since 1982.
Hurricane Isaias “could be a gigantic event. It’s the worst time something like this could happen in 25 years,” said Robert Yawger, director of energy futures at Mizuho Securities.
The actual impact of Isaias will depend on the storm’s path and intensity.
Current forecasts call for the storm to hit east of New Orleans, a major refining hub, which should spare vital energy infrastructure from the storm’s worst.
Still, major oil producers including Shell, Chevron and BP have evacuated non-essential personnel from oil platforms in the Gulf and curtailed production .
As of midday Wednesday, about 512,000 barrels per day of Gulf of Mexico oil production had been shut in, according to the federal agency Marine Minerals Administration.
That amounts to about 25% of the region’s production. And about 16% of current natural gas production in the Gulf of Mexico has been sidelined.
The risk is that the storm’s damage could squeeze supply chains even more, further raising historically high prices.
The Iran war, combined with Ukrainian drone attacks in Russia and export restrictions in China, have catapulted diesel prices to all-time highs. Gasoline was more than $4.40 per gallon last week and has never been this expensive at this time of year.
How gas station owners set their prices
About 2.7 million barrels per day, or 14%, of America’s refining capacity, lie within or near the projected of the path of the storm, according to Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates.
Lipow said he expects at least some refineries in the New Orleans/Baton Rouge and Mississippi/Alabama regions will have to slow down how much oil they turn into gasoline, diesel and jet fuel.
Tankers delivering oil to refineries and loading fuel out of refineries could get delayed as well. This would particularly impact Florida because the state relies on shipments of fuel from the Gulf Coast.
“There is no slack in the system to make up for lost refinery capacity. Lost production will have to come out of already low commercial inventories,” Lipow wrote in an email.
Those commercial inventories have been whittled away.
Gasoline stockpiles recently fell to their lowest seasonal record since 2012, according to federal data.
Distillate inventories, which include mostly diesel, are at their lowest level for early October since tracking started in the early 1980s.
Not only that, but the Strategic Petroleum Reserve has been aggressively drained to ease the energy shock. The SPR now holds about 283 million barrels of crude, the least since 1982 when the emergency reserve was being filled during the Reagan administration.
Refineries in the Middle East have been damaged by the Iran war, or have struggled to get shipments out to the rest of the world. Refineries in Russia have been destroyed or damaged by drone attacks. And China, seeking to avoid fuel shortages, has restricted its exports.
US refineries, operating at about 95% of their capacity, are one of the remaining key sources for the global fuel supply.
“It would be a disaster if US refining capacity has to come off the market. It would basically force a diesel export ban,” said Yawger, the Mizuho executive, who added that he is not in favor of restricting US diesel exports .
Much depends on the intensity of the storm, including the severity of flooding and wind damage. Isaias could peak as a Category 2 storm with 110 mph winds by early Friday, but is expected to weaken somewhat before landfall.
Even with a Category 1 hurricane, it can take a week to return refining operations to normal.

articles.title_orig: 10-year Treasury yield is little changed as Fed's Waller says more hikes needed, investors await 30-year auction
articles.title_zh: 10-year Treasury yield is little changed as Fed's Waller says more hikes needed, investors await 30-year auction
articles.content_orig:
The yield on the 10-year Treasury was relatively unchanged on Thursday as traders digested comments from a top Federal Reserve official along with another long-dated bond auction.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield was last down 4 basis points at 5.237% after reaching its highest level since 2002 this week. The 30-year Treasury bond yield fell nearly 5 basis points to 5.614% after trading around a 24-year high recently.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Fed Governor Christopher Waller said on Thursday that more hikes are needed to bring inflation down after around 5-and-a-half years above the central bank's 2% target, but suggested rates did not need to rise immediately.
"The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings," Waller told a Central Bank of Turkey forum in Istanbul. "But they should be in place in an acceptable period of time."
His comments initially sent yields higher on the day. However, rates gave back those advances after President Donald Trump said the U.S. won't attack Iran until after the November midterm election . Yields also pulled back after a solid 30-year Treasury bond auction.
The department sold $22 billion in 30-year paper, with indirect bidders — which include central banks — scooping up 72.3% of the sale. That's above a 10-auction average of 68%. Direct bidders, including institutional investors, took 20.9% of the auction, just below an average of 22%. The yield at auction ease 5.618%.
That marks the final auction of the week. The department sold $58 billion in 3-year notes on Tuesday and another $39 billion in 10-year notes.
Thursday's sale "was decent but nowhere close to as good as the 10 yr auction yesterday," wrote Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer of One Point BFG Wealth Partners.
— CNBC's Brianna Bernath contributed reporting.

articles.content_orig:
Observers on both sides are braced for more turbulence – and mainly hope Beijing and Brussels can avoid a full-blown trade conflict
As China and the European Union began a fresh round of trade talks in Beijing on Thursday, observers on both sides appeared to agree on one thing: a big breakthrough was unlikely.
Chinese firms based in Europe said they hoped the talks could achieve some “limited progress” to help stabilise the trade relationship, while European analysts remained cautious about the potential outcome.
“They’re bound to get some results,” said a Chinese source with knowledge of the talks, adding that EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic “will not go home empty-handed”.
The China Chamber of Commerce to the EU called on both sides to make full use of the Trade and Investment Consultations (TIC) mechanism to manage differences, push for solutions and send clearer signals to businesses.

articles.title_orig: Long-Deployed Aircraft Carrier U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln Set for Homecoming
articles.title_zh: Long-Deployed Aircraft Carrier U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln Set for Homecoming
articles.content_orig:
The USS Abraham Lincoln is returning home to San Diego Thursday after supporting the Iran war during a record long deployment of 265 uninterrupted days at sea that included reports of deteriorating conditions among its crew.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth flew out to the carrier on Wednesday to give the crew the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a unit can receive that is typically reserved for significant achievement in combat.
Hegseth pushed back against what he said were efforts to turn the "Lincoln into some sort of a symbol, a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission."
He said that "what makes the U.S. military and the U.S. Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you're resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless."
Hegseth told the crew that President Donald Trump "tracked your activities from day one and couldn't be more proud of what you executed."
The carrier drew national attention following reports of stress among the crew and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products, during its Iran war mission.
The Navy initially downplayed any problems, and Trump commented in August that the Lincoln's lengthy deployment was "not nearly long enough."
The carrier had left San Diego in November and arrived in the Middle East in January. U.S. and Israeli forces launched airstrikes against Iran on Feb. 28.
Navy leaders, however, eventually acknowledged there were some issues aboard.
In August, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the Lincoln maintained adequate food supplies, but because combat operations limited resupply opportunities, meal options were reduced from two to one for a short time. He said in a letter to a Democratic lawmaker seeking information that four nutritionally balanced meals were served daily.
After more than 10 months at sea, the Lincoln's crew got a stop in Thailand early last month on the way back from the Middle East.
Extended naval deployments can wear on service members who are away from home for long periods and increase strain on the ship and its equipment.
The Navy told lawmakers that eight sailors attempted suicide during the record-setting deployment, though experts say that number is low in a strike group of 6,000 sailors over 10 months.
According to the citation that Hegseth read to the crew, the Lincoln and its strike group executed 3,693 combat missions, delivered 1.37 million pounds of ordnance, launched 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles, shot down 77 one-way attack drones, sank 64 Iranian warships, destroyed 21 anti-ship cruise missiles and defended against four fast-attack craft and explosive-carrying ships.
The Lincoln, which set a record for days in between ports of call, is the second carrier to endure an unusually long deployment to support the war against Iran and to receive the Presidential Unit Citation afterward.
Hegseth in May met the crew of the USS Gerald R. Ford during its return from a 326-day deployment — the longest for an aircraft carrier in the past 50 years and a record in the post-Vietnam War era.
Another carrier, the usually Asia-based USS George Washington, relieved the Lincoln in the Middle East in August.

articles.title_orig: What impact Old Vine Seal can have on world’s oldest vineyards
articles.title_zh: What impact Old Vine Seal can have on world’s oldest vineyards
articles.content_orig:
What started way back in 2010 as a grassroots, volunteer effort by wine critic Jancis Robinson MW and her team to record all the vineyards in the world that qualify as old vines has developed into the full blown Old Vine Registry that now includes close to 5,000 producers. It has now introduced the OV Seal to give those producers the chance to promote, on their label, how old their vines are and help spread the word to wine drinkers about the importance and significance of old vines. Alder Yarrow, architect and manager of the OVR explains what he hopes the new seal can achieve.
Tell us about the new seal initiative you have introduced?
The creation and growth of the Old Vine Registry has always been predicated on the idea that we can’t preserve or value what we don’t know about. So our first and ongoing goal has been to catalogue old vine vineyards everywhere.
In addition to knowing they exist, however, to keep them in the ground we have to make sure they remain economically sustainable for those who farm them, and one of the ways to do this is to drive increased awareness and sales of the wines that get made from old vineyards.
In order to do that, the Old Vine Registry had to get out of the internet and into the real world, and the OVR Seal is our attempt to do that—to start having the conversation about old vines at the shelf level.
What do you hope to achieve with it that you can’t currently do with the Registry?
The Old Vine Registery now has the records of nearly 5,000 producers in its database
By allowing registered producers to put the OVR Seal on their bottles, we are giving wineries around the world the chance to declare how old their vineyards are and to give interested consumers a destination to learn more, in the form of the Old Vine Registry listing for their vineyard.
This offers an opportunity for consumers to learn and engage in a way that the use of words such as “vieilles vignes” or “old vines” don’t offer. Also unlike those terms, which mostly have no legal meaning or regulation guiding their usage around the world, the OVR Seal offers a more concrete and legitimate declaration that a vineyard truly is old.
What do producers or winemakers need to do in order to use the seal?
In order to use the seal, producers must have their vineyard(s) listed in the Old Vine Registry, which is free and easy to do. Once that has occurred, a producer must simply pay a one-time fee of $300 to get access to seal artwork that corresponds to the age of their registered vines.
They are then free to use the seal on their packaging and digital marketing materials associated with wines made from their registered vineyard.
You are launching the seal with a few initial producers - who are they and why have they come on first?
We teased the fact that the Seal was coming back in June, and a number of wineries immediately reached out asking how they might get access to the seal. We offered the opportunity to get early access to the seal to all the producers who made such inquiries, and eleven of them stepped up and said they wanted to particpate.
Derek Mossman Knapp of Chile's Garage Wine Company is one of the first producers to take on the Old Vine Registery seal
Our launch partners are: Seghesio Family Vineyards and Bedrock Wine Company in Sonoma, Garage Wine Company in Chile, Versado and Ciclo Andino in Mendoza, AYA Estate in Bulgaria, Sown Estate in Napa, Woldridge Creek Winery in Oregon, Methymnaeos Organic Vineyards in Greece, Plaimont in Gascony, and Tenuta Santa Maria in Soave.
These are all wineries that have, at a minimum, made commitments to making old vineyards a key part of their philosophical approach to winemaking. Some of them, like Bedrock Wine Company or Garage Wine Company, go much further than that, as shepherds of some of the world’s oldest and most storied vineyards.
How will producers be able to use it in their marketing and on their labels?
The seal is available for use in the context of products and marketing that are specific to one or more vineyards that are recorded in the Old Vine Registry. The age-specific seal can be used on wine packaging if 85% of the grapes come from one or more registered vineyards that are at least as old as the age-mark on the seal. In the same fashion, the seal may also be used on technical sheets or sell-sheets or even e-commerce product pages for specific individual wines.
We also anticipate producers using the seal in the context of marketing a specific registered vineyard, perhaps on websites or in print marketing, or even by putting a sign in the vineyard itself. We’re really open to however wineries want to use the seal, provided it is always in the context of mentioning or referencing a specific vineyard rather than generic marketing about the brand as a whole.
What percentage of producers who are in the registry do you hope to sign up to use the seal?
Examples of how producers are using the Old Vine Registry seal on their labels
We honestly have no idea how many wineries are going to be excited about this seal. Many producers don’t even know that their vineyards are listed in the Old Vine Registry. Of the 5,474 unique producers listed in the Old Vine Registry, if we got 10% of them using the seal, I would consider that a smashing success.
Is there a registration cost to use the seal?
Yes, we’ve settled on a one-time $300 registration cost to use the seal. This amount was chosen to be affordable to even the smallest producers, while making sure that everyone who registers has at least a little skin in the game. The fee is not a recurring subscription, and registered producers are free to use the seal providing they have a qualified, registered vineyard that is still in the ground.
For those that don’t know the Old Vine Registry - what are your primary objectives?
As a registered nonprofit, Old Vine Registry exists to catalog the world’s vineyards over 35 years-old. Once recorded, we hope to drive awareness of and an increased appreciation for the value of old vineyards with the hopes that this leads to increased sales of the wines they produce, and ultimately their preservation.
How do you hope the seal will help your overall work?
The seal will hopefully become a point of difference and an opportunity for conversation between producers and their customers that brings the idea of old vines and what makes them special into the spotlight. If using the seal can get some of wine lovers to be more curious about old vines and why they matter we’re on our way to the ultimate outcome, which would be to create a legitimate commercial category for old vine wines.
We’re working towards a day when every serious wine list, every retailer, importer, and distributor, should have an old-vine section that is used to highlight the incredible wines made from the world’s old vineyards.
What other initiatives do you have planned for the OVR?
Alder Yarrow is manager of the Old Vine Registry - a role he is prepared to do on a voluntary basis
Once the OVR Seal program is up and running smoothly, we’re going to go back to making improvements to the Old Vine Registry website that will make it an even more valuable resource for the industry and academia. This will include publishing analysis on the increasingly sizeable set of data that the registry collects and different ways of interrogating that data.
And of course, we’re going to continue adding more and more vineyards to the registry. We’re not anywhere close to having even a quarter of the world’s old vineyards catalogued.
In October of 2024, the OIV published Resolution OIV-VITI 703-2024 which for the first time established an official definition of what “old vines” means for European wine. More importantly that resolution recommended "the cataloguing of old vineyards and old grapevines" and "to make openly available official data from the vineyard register to draw up vineyard maps and ascertain the age of vineyards.”

articles.title_orig: ‘Nature can recover’: Inside the race to rescue world’s crisis-hit wildlife
articles.title_zh: ‘Nature can recover’: Inside the race to rescue world’s crisis-hit wildlife
articles.content_orig:
Beneath the dense forest canopy of Uganda’s Bwindi Impenetrable National Park, a troop of gorillas is being quietly observed by a group of tourists who have each paid $800 for the privilege of the experience.
In villages around the park, a thriving economy has grown off the back of the gorillas’ presence here, from the sale of wood carvings to visitors and the provision of accommodation for up to 40,000 tourists a year.
In the national park, which sprawls along the edge of the Rift Valley and the border with the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), there are many local jobs for rangers and guides.
But deeper into the forest, more mountain gorillas live away from human contact, quietly enhancing the natural world around them through their daily routines of foraging, nest building and dispersing seeds.
And, crucially, by increasing their own populations.
In the 1980s, the mountain gorilla was on the fast track to extinction. Now, there are more than 1,100 living in thriving populations in Uganda, Rwanda and the DRC.
Theirs is a story of conservation success that spills beyond the species themselves, into the nature they live in, and the human communities they exist alongside.
“The mountain gorilla story shows us that conservation can work,” Tara Stoinski of the Dian Fossey Gorilla Fund tells Al Jazeera. “It’s a really important example of the effort that’s needed to make that happen – decades of sustained conservation action that includes direct protection, science-informed management and meaningful community support and involvement.”
This is welcome news for a natural world beset by crisis.
According to this year’s Living Planet Report by the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF), over the past 52 years, there has been a 73 percent decline in the average size of monitored wildlife populations. Across the world, habitats have been degraded and lost as overexploitation, climate change, pollution and invasive species take their toll.
But the report also highlights important recoveries in populations of green turtles, bluefin tuna, tigers and Southern African elephants. “For too long nature has been undervalued,” says Andrew Terry, chief conservation officer at the Zoological Society of London, who helped produce the report. “But these declines are not inevitable and change is possible. Nature can recover, and these stories are a powerful reminder of this.”
The WWF says these conservation successes demonstrate how international partnerships drive results. Intergovernmental commitments from tiger range countries, including India, Bhutan, Nepal, Laos and China, helped increase global wild tiger numbers by more than 70 percent between 2010 and 2025.
In 2025, the green sea turtle became the first marine turtle ever to be downlisted from “endangered” to “least concern” on the International Union for the Conservation of Nature Red List. That reflected 50 years of species research, active protection of nesting females and eggs, measures to reduce fishing gear and sustained community engagement.
Professor Brendon Godley is a leading conservation scientist at the University of Exeter and the Sharjah Marine Research Centre in the United Arab Emirates and has spent much of his career dedicated to researching and protecting sea turtles. “Conservation success stories are hugely important because they demonstrate that declines are not inevitable,” he tells Al Jazeera.
“The recovery of species such as green turtles shows that when science, policy, enforcement and public support align, populations can rebound, sometimes remarkably so. However, they are not grounds for complacency.”
Indeed, these conservation triumphs are small battles won in an ongoing war against the degradation of nature. The WWF’s Living Planet Report highlights the three systems that are primarily driving the destruction of nature: the global food system, which is the leading cause of habitat loss as areas are cleared to grow crops; the energy system, which fuels climate change through burning fossil fuels; and the finance system, which bankrolls harmful activities, for example, large-scale infrastructure or mining projects.
Kirsten Schuijt, director general of WWF, says these industries and systems need to be transformed. “Progress is already under way,” she tells Al Jazeera. “Not everywhere, and not yet at the scale required, but enough to demonstrate that change is possible.”
The return of a species can have a powerful effect. In 2010, Atlantic bluefin tuna populations had declined by 80 percent and the species was listed as endangered. They had disappeared from much of their historical range, including UK waters. Yet today they are returning in numbers not witnessed in generations, perhaps ever.
“What makes this story particularly powerful is that the recovery is visible,” says Tom Horton, research fellow at the University of Exeter. “Coastal communities, fishers and sea-users who had never seen a bluefin tuna in British waters are now encountering them regularly. It transforms conservation from an abstract concept into something tangible.”
These successes serve as inspiration for other conservation projects in the fight against species decline, like that of the largest primate on Earth, the critically endangered Grauer’s Gorilla. Its home range lies within the vast remote forests of the DRC, living in a landscape beset by instability and habitat loss. Its numbers have dropped by an estimated 60 percent to just 6,800 today.
Urbain Ngobobo, country director for the Dian Fossey Fund in the DRC, explains that the challenge of restoring numbers there is significant but so is the opportunity.
“Every forest we help communities protect,” he says, “every gorilla we are able to monitor and every young Congolese person who develops the skills to become a conservation leader, represents progress.
“That is where hope comes from – not from assuming the future will be easy, but from knowing that our actions today can change what is possible tomorrow.”
_src_links: ‘Nature can recover’: Inside the race to rescue world’s crisis-hit wildlife

articles.title_orig: Oil prices rise sharply on Middle East tensions and US hurricane threat
articles.title_zh: Oil prices rise sharply on Middle East tensions and US hurricane threat
articles.content_orig:
Global bond market sell-off continues and stocks fall amid another wave of potential strikes against Iran
Business live – latest updates
Oil prices have risen sharply amid fears about escalating tensions in the Middle East and a squeeze on production from the threat of a hurricane off the US coast.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose by 3.8% to $104 a barrel on Thursday, triggering a wave of selling in the global bond and stock markets.
The White House has asked the Pentagon to draw up options for strikes against Iran before the US midterm elections, according to a report in The Atlantic. The report cited unnamed officials in Donald Trump’s administration who said the size and targets of potential strikes, and whether they will go ahead, are still being debated.
The report has weakened hopes that Trump will refrain from escalating the conflict with Iran before the midterm polls next month. A “limited operation” could be followed up by more substantial action after the midterms, it states.
Another wave of strikes against Iran represents further risk to oil supply from the Middle East, with the US-Israeli war against Tehran now entering its eighth month. Attacks on tankers in the strait of Hormuz reached their highest levels of ⁠the war, ⁠cutting ​traffic through the waterway and deepening fears about supply.
The latest attack came ⁠on Wednesday, when a tanker was hit by multiple projectiles off the north coast of Qatar , causing casualties, according to ​the United Kingdom Maritime ‌Trade Operations.
Oil prices also rose in response to a squeeze on production in the Gulf of Mexico, after the tropical storm Isaias strengthened to become the first hurricane of the Atlantic season.
Shell and Chevron both said they were shutting down production as the storm approached the region, forecast to make landfall on Friday or Saturday.
Maersk, the Danish shipping group, added to worries around rising energy prices on Thursday after it said it was increasing its emergency fuel surcharge on all its export collections and import deliveries. The rise in energy prices has fed fears about inflation, reinforcing expectations that central banks will have to raise their interest rates in order to control rising prices.
A sell-off in global bond markets continued on Thursday.
In the UK, the yield on the 30-year gilt – the benchmark for the cost of long-term government borrowing – rose by 3 basis points to 6.0117%, after touching 6.036% on Wednesday, the highest since January 1998.
The 10-year gilt yield rose by 5 basis points to 5.48%, approaching the 5.5% mark, returning to levels not seen since July 2007.
after newsletter promotion
In France, which has been hit particularly hard over worries around its rising debt and growing spending , the 10-year yield rose by 6 basis points to 4.931%, just behind the 24-year high of 4.994% it hit last week. Yields rise when prices fall.
The German 10-year yield, the benchmark for European debt, rose by 2 basis points to 3.504%.
The yield on the US 10-year treasury, which is widely considered the best quality government debt on the market, rose by 5 basis points to 5.331%.
Global stocks also fell, with Japan’s Nikkei share index falling 1.4% and the South Korean Kospi down 2.6%.
In Europe, the Stoxx Europe 600, which tracks the biggest companies on the continent, dropped 0.9%. The UK’s FTSE 100 slipped by 0.4% in early trading on Thursday.

articles.title_orig: New global roadmap launched to tackle hypertension in pregnancy, a leading cause of maternal and newborn deaths
articles.title_zh: New global roadmap launched to tackle hypertension in pregnancy, a leading cause of maternal and newborn deaths
articles.content_orig:
The World Health Organization (WHO) and partners today launched a new global roadmap to tackle hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, including pre-eclampsia , which affect millions of women every year. These disorders remain among the leading causes of death and serious illness for pregnant women and their babies, with tragic long-term impact on their families.
Hypertensive disorders complicate an estimated 10–15% of pregnancies worldwide. They account for around 16% of maternal deaths globally, resulting in an estimated 42 000 deaths each year, as well as more than 500 000 stillbirths and newborn deaths.
In many countries, women still lack reliable access to basic blood-pressure measurement, urine protein testing and essential medicines, including aspirin, antihypertensives and magnesium sulfate. Weak referral systems, shortages of trained health workers and limited emergency obstetric services can further delay life-saving care.
“Pre-eclampsia can develop in any pregnancy. Whether it becomes fatal depends on whether a woman's blood pressure was checked in time, and whether quality emergency care was within reach when it turned severe,” said Dr Pascale Allotey, Director of WHO’s Department of Sexual, Reproductive, Maternal, Child, Adolescent Health and Ageing. “This roadmap  brings together research, medicines, clinical guidance, health systems and political action so that a woman’s chances of surviving pregnancy and having a baby do not depend on where she lives.”
Launched at the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine Global Conference, the Global roadmap for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy from 2026 to 2035 and beyond sets out coordinated actions across research and innovation, global clinical guidance, access to medicines and diagnostics, implementation, advocacy and accountability.
The roadmap highlights a striking innovation gap between the scale of the problem and the lack of medicines specifically developed and approved by regulators for the prevention or treatment of pre-eclampsia or eclampsia. Research investment has largely focused on diagnostics, with chronic underinvestment in new preventive and treatment options.
To change this, WHO brought together more than 140 partners at a global summit in May 2026 to identify and answer 20 priority research questions to guide future investment that will help predict, detect and treat hypertensive disorders in pregnancy. In low- and middle-income countries, gaps in antenatal care, medicines, diagnostics, trained health workers and emergency services mean women are more likely to develop severe complications or die. Women affected by poverty, humanitarian crises, geographic isolation and other challenges face particularly high risks.
Pre-eclampsia can also have consequences for mothers long after childbirth. Women affected by hypertensive disorders of pregnancy face increased risks later in life of chronic hypertension, cardiovascular disease, stroke and kidney disease, while children exposed during pregnancy can face increased risks associated with preterm birth and longer-term cardiovascular and metabolic disease.
WHO asks governments, funders, researchers, health professionals, industry, civil society and development partners to align investment and action around one goal: ensuring that proven interventions and future innovations reach the women and babies who need them most.
Dedicated to the well-being of all people and guided by science, WHO leads and champions global efforts to give everyone, everywhere, an equal chance at a safe and healthy life. We are the United Nations’ agency for health that connects nations, partners and people in more than 150 locations – leading the world’s response to health emergencies, preventing disease, addressing the root causes of health issues and expanding access to medicines and health care. Our mission is to support all countries to promote, provide and protect health. The theme of World Health Day 2026, “Together for health. Stand with science”, marks a year-long campaign to highlight science as the foundation for protecting health and well-being worldwide.

articles.content_orig:
The capital injection marks the firm’s second share placement since its Hong Kong listing in January, following a previous round in July
Shares of artificial intelligence chipmaker Shanghai Biren Technology tumbled more than 12 per cent in Hong Kong on Thursday amid plans to raise HK$4 billion (US$510 million) through a share placement, as competition with other Chinese Nvidia challengers intensifies.
The sell-off followed a stock exchange filing by the Hong Kong-listed company on late Wednesday, which revealed it had engaged placing agents on a “best effort” basis to issue 130 million new shares at HK$31.08 apiece.
The offering price represents a roughly 10 per cent discount to the stock’s closing price of HK$34.44 on the previous day. The new shares would account for around 5 per cent of its total issued shares as of Wednesday, according to the filing.
Biren shares dropped to as low as HK$30.24 before closing down 11.9 per cent at HK$30.36 on Thursday.

With their public mandates, financial resources and ability to leverage additional investment, MDBs could play an important role in financing the transition to low-carbon, climate-resilient and sustainable economies. Yet concerns remain about continued MDB support for fossil fuel projects and other investments that contribute to ecological destruction, carbon-intensive development and climate vulnerability, as well as about debt-based financing that place additional burdens on countries already facing climate and debt crises.
This hybrid event will examine where MDB money is going, what kinds of energy systems and development pathways it is helping to finance, and who bears the costs and risks. A case study will illustrate the social, ecological and financial impacts of MDB-supported investments. The discussion will then turn to pathways for change, including legal and accountability tools that communities, civil society and affected peoples can use to challenge harmful financing and hold public financiers to account.

articles.title_orig: Indonesian haze makes Singapore the most polluted city in the world
articles.title_zh: Indonesian haze makes Singapore the most polluted city in the world
articles.content_orig:
Singapore had the most polluted air of any city in the world on Wednesday as smoke from wildfires in Indonesia blanketed Southeast Asia and forced schools in Malaysia to close.
Air quality in the city fell into the "very unhealthy" range on Wednesday afternoon, according to the Swiss air-quality monitoring company IQAir, which ranked it first for pollution globally.
The Malaysian capital Kuala Lumpur had held the top spot earlier in the day.
The National Environment Agency, which measures air quality on its own Pollutant Standards Index, put air in all five regions of Singapore at unhealthy levels. That's the index's band of 101 to 200, below its "very unhealthy" band. At 7am on Thursday, the agency's 24-hour reading stood at 109 in central Singapore and 111 in the east.
The agency forecast dry conditions over most of the southern part of Southeast Asia in the next few days, which it said would keep the risk of fires and haze elevated.
In Malaysia, all schools, kindergartens and childcare centres in Batu Pahat, in the southern state of Johor, nearly 140km northwest of Singapore, were ordered closed after the district's Air Pollutant Index reached 203, in the "very unhealthy" band, on Tuesday morning, the local disaster management committee said, adding that reopening would depend on air quality readings. The order affects nearly 200 schools, kindergartens and nurseries in Batu Pahat.
A board displaying air quality shows hazardous levels of PM10 and PM2.5 airborne pollutants as thick smoke and haze shrouds the city of Pontianak in West Kalimantan (AFP/Getty)
The haze has been caused by uncontrolled fires in Indonesia , where the practice of clearing farmland by burning has combined with an intensifying El Nino , a natural climate cycle drying out the landscape. The number of hotspots last month was the highest since 2015, according to SiPongi, the fire-monitoring platform run by the Indonesian forestry ministry.
In 2015, the regional haze caused widespread disruption and diplomatic tensions between Indonesia and its neighbours.
The campaign group Greenpeace identified over 20 palm oil, pulp and sugar companies whose land concessions contained sources of smoke from the fires, including several with links to Malaysia and Singapore.
The haze arrives days before the Singapore Grand Prix , the Formula One race, kicks off on Friday. The race's organiser, Singapore GP, said on Tuesday it would work closely with the relevant agencies "to assess the situation before making any collective decisions regarding the event" if the haze caused problems with visibility, public health or operations.
A Formula One spokesperson said conditions weren't at any level of concern, Bloomberg reported.
Last week organisers of the Standard Chartered Marathon in Kuala Lumpur cancelled a children's race due to health concerns but went ahead with other races, including the full and half marathons. In 2015, the marathon had been cancelled.

articles.title_orig: World’s largest penguin colony loses two-thirds of its population
articles.title_zh: World’s largest penguin colony loses two-thirds of its population
articles.content_orig:
The world's largest penguin colony on a remote island near Antarctica has suffered a sharp decline in numbers , most likely because of the climate crisis, a new study has found.
Researchers from the British Antarctic Survey found a 63 per cent drop in occupied chinstrap penguin nests between 2011 and 2025 on Zavodovski, a volcanic island in the South Sandwich Islands.
The number of breeding chinstraps fell from 1.09 million to 402,000, according to the study published on Wednesday in the journal Current Biology .
This means Zavodovski island is no longer the world's largest penguin colony. The title now belongs to Cape Adare on the other side of Antarctica in the Ross Sea.
The South Sandwich Islands, a British overseas territory, are a remote archipelago north of Antarctica, and Zavodovski is the northernmost of them. It is twice the size of Gibraltar and lies 2,000km from the nearest permanent human settlement.
The researchers sailed for more than a fortnight to reach it, using drone surveys, aerial photography and tracking devices fitted to penguins.
For years the island appeared to buck the trend of chinstrap decline reported across Antarctica and its surrounding islands. Now, the researchers say, it is suffering the highest rate of chinstrap decline in the world.
"This is a worrying decline for chinstraps, which have specialist diets and specific ocean temperature preferences," said Professor Norman Ratcliffe, penguin ecologist at the survey who led the study. He described the fall as "an enormous population crash".
Chinstraps, named for the black line that runs cheek-to-cheek under the beak, feed on Antarctic krill, small shrimp-like animals that make up most of their diet.
Tracking data shows the penguins prefer to feed in cooler waters to the northwest of the island, where they would expect to find krill. "The problem is, with waters warming, the krill have moved southwards into the Weddell Sea ," Prof Ratcliffe explained.
"Sea-ice cover to the south and a lack of suitable islands for nesting prevents chinstraps from following the food."
Chinstrap penguins on Deception Island in the western Antarctic Peninsula (AFP/Getty)
Macaroni penguins on the other hand saw their population increase by 28 per cent between 2011 and 2016, from about 338,000 to 433,000, and hold steady thereafter. So, they now outnumber chinstraps on the island.
Macaronis, unlike chinstraps, enjoy a more varied diet and switch to fish and other crustaceans when krill becomes scarcer. Tracking data shows them feeding mainly in warmer waters to the northeast of the island.
"Our data shows that the cold-adapted Antarctic chinstrap species are no longer thriving beside their sub-Antarctic neighbours," Prof Ratcliffe said. "It's the biggest change in community composition ever observed at a single location in Antarctica, which provides further evidence of how rapid warming in the Antarctic is impacting unique and sensitive ecosystems."
He told the Guardian that the rise in the macaroni population was small comfort because all penguins would run out of space if current trends continued. "Each ecosystem could be regarded as like a giant Jenga set," he said, "and every component that you remove increases the risk of ecosystems collapsing completely."
The researchers tested other explanations for the decline before pointing to the climate crisis. The island's volcano, Mount Curry, erupted in March 2016 and deposited smoke and ash over the lower slopes, but the study found the decline began earlier.
"The decline in chinstrap colony area was in progress prior to the eruption and continued at a constant rate thereafter," the study noted. The data also showed that chinstraps avoided the area where ash and lava landed.
Gentoo penguins and seals at the Yankee Harbour in the South Shetland Islands, Antarctica, on 6 March 2016 (AFP/Getty)
The researchers also ruled out competition for nesting space as an explanation because the island contained enough breeding habitat. They said krill fishing was unlikely to be a main cause because harvesting was banned in the marine protected area around the island, though they said it was unclear how fishing in connected waters was affecting the wider supply of food.
They ruled out competition from humpback whales as well. The whales do eat huge quantities of krill but also help boost their production by fertilising the marine plants they feed on.
The study, however, noted that rising competition from macaroni penguins likely made the chinstrap decline worse.
The South Sandwich islands are home to almost a third of the world's chinstraps and the researchers say the decline here, together with falls elsewhere in Antarctica, may be enough to move the species from the category of least concern to endangered on the global list of threatened species kept by the International Union for Conservation of Nature .
Emperor penguins were declared endangered earlier this year after sea ice loss caused large population declines, according to Euronews.
Dr Peter Fretwell, a survey researcher specialising in remote sensing of penguins, said the study was further evidence of the warming climate affecting even the most remote parts of the planet.
"The South Sandwich Islands are far from any humans, home to almost a third of the world's chinstrap penguins," he said, "but not even they can escape the impacts of climate change."
_src_links: World’s largest penguin colony loses two-thirds of its population

articles.title_orig: Everything announced at Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra event
articles.title_zh: Everything announced at Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra event
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft just wrapped up a big Windows and Surface-focused keynote in San Francisco.
The biggest announcement was arguably the release details about the Surface Laptop Ultra , its new laptop that’s powered by Nvidia’s RTX Spark Arm-based chip. The machine will start at $2,599 for a configuration with an 8-core CPU, 24GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage, and it will be released on October 16th. The laptop also has built-in magnetic USB-C charging instead of the proprietary Surface Connect magnetic charging port. The Verge ’s Tom Warren published a deep dive all about the new laptop . Microsoft also announced that the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, a mini PC for developers, is available for preorder for $5,999 ahead of shipping in November.
In addition, Microsoft shared details about some updates coming to Windows , including “Hybrid Intelligence” features that lets Copilot use files on your Windows PC to take actions and a new search experience that lets you do quick actions from the search bar.
You can catch up with all of our coverage from the event right here.
Before Microsoft releases a laptop to the public, it needs to put the device through its paces. That all happens inside a windowless, warehouse-like lab on the company’s Redmond, Washington, campus, where the team developing Surface devices programs robots to press their buttons thousands of times, pelts devices with radio waves from giant antennas, and builds contraptions that drop objects from increasingly daring heights to see whether the products can hold up.
Its latest laptop, the product I’m here to see, really needs to hold up. The Surface Laptop Ultra isn’t just another high-end config of the Surface Laptop, it’s the debut platform for Nvidia’s RTX Spark — Nvidia’s entrance into the world of Arm-based PC chips, and a chance to blow expectations out of the water when it comes to what a Windows laptop is capable of.
Tough typo spotted in today’s Surface Laptop Ultra event.
The first array of laptops powered by Nvidia’s new RTX Spark chip are designed to compete with high-end MacBook Pros — and they’ve got some high-end prices to match.
At today’s Windows and Surface event, Microsoft showed off an upgrade to its Copilot AI system that will give it access to local files on your PC and the ability to take actions across the OS. It’s part of an idea Microsoft is calling “Hybrid Intelligence,” where apps and tools rely on a mix of local and cloud AI models to accomplish tasks efficiently.
To show off how Hybrid Intelligence works, Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s EVP of Copilot, walked through a video demo onstage asking Microsoft’s Autopilot tool to help with filing taxes. Andreou told the AI agent that he got an email from his accountant and asked Autopilot to get her what she needs. Autopilot then used Hybrid Intelligence to search across different folders to find the documents, rename the files, zip them into a folder, and draft an email to send to the accountant with the zip file attached.
Months after revealing its Surface Laptop Ultra , Microsoft has announced that the Nvidia RTX Spark-equipped device will launch on October 16th. Pricing starts at $2,599 for the base configuration, featuring an 18-core CPU, 24GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage.
The Surface Laptop Ultra ships with a 15-inch HDR touchscreen display with up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness, along with a larger trackpad that supports haptic feedback. The device uses Nvidia’s new RTX Spark chip , an Arm-based processor with up to 128GB of unified memory. Both Microsoft and Nvidia are positioning RTX Spark laptops at the very premium end of the laptop market, designed for high performance across creative software, gaming, and local AI tasks.
Microsoft’s Nvidia-powered Surface RTX Spark Dev Box is available for preorder now and is slated to ship in November for just about $6,000. It’s pricier than the DGX Spark mini PC Nvidia launched last year, but PC prices have been climbing due to shortages of RAM and other components .
The Dev Box’s flat, 3D-printed anodized aluminum chassis doubles as a heatsink and resembles the top vents on an Xbox Series X. It was introduced alongside the new Surface Laptop Ultra and runs on Nvidia’s Arm-based RTX Spark platform and 128GB of unified memory. With that much memory, along with a 100-watt thermal envelope and Nvidia’s Tensor cores, you could probably get an impressive gaming experience on the Dev Box. But as its name suggests, it’s mainly aimed at developers. It’s optimized for running local AI, including “models exceeding 120B parameters,” for tasks like testing AI models, prototyping AI agents, or running AI coding tools on-device.
Microsoft has created a magnetic charging solution for its Surface Laptop Ultra that uses USB-C. After scrapping its proprietary Surface Connect magnetic charging on its smaller Surface devices last year, the Surface Laptop Ultra has a charging cable that attaches magnetically to the right side USB-C port.
During Microsoft’s Windows event on Wednesday, Windows and Surface chief Pavan Davuluri said that you can just “bring the connector close, and it snaps right into place.“ It’s still a proprietary solution, but the USB-C port it slots into still works for video, data, and other USB-C connectivity like you’d expect. Microsoft is calling it Magnetic Connect, and I’m surprised the company hasn’t shortened that to Mag-C.
Meta’s new AI agent will be getting a native app on Windows, Windows and Surface chief Pavan Davuluri announced at today’s event. No timeline on when, though. Meta launched a Mac Muse app in September .
Tom Warren and Sean Hollister
We’re in San Francisco today to hear what’s next for Windows and Surface. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and Windows and Surface chief Pavan Davuluri will all be holding a “conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC.”
Microsoft and Nvidia have been working together on the new RTX Spark platform, which is focused on boosting local AI models, creative apps, and even gaming on a series of new laptops. Nvidia’s GPU expertise is getting squeezed into laptops like the Surface Laptop Ultra, and we’re about to find out exactly what it’s capable of.

articles.title_orig: Kiplimo and Feysa return to defend Chicago titles
articles.title_zh: Kiplimo and Feysa return to defend Chicago titles
articles.content_orig:
Jacob Kiplimo and Hawi Feysa in Chicago ( © Bank of America Chicago Marathon Kevin Morris )
Jacob Kiplimo and Hawi Feysa will return to the Bank of America Chicago Marathon to defend their titles against deep international fields at the World Athletics Platinum Label road race on Sunday (11).
Kiplimo heads back to Chicago having significantly improved his marathon credentials since winning there 12 months ago, while Feysa faces a women’s field that includes former world record-holder Brigid Kosgei and two-time Boston champion Sharon Lokedi.
Kiplimo won in Chicago last year in 2:02:23, finishing more than a minute ahead of Kenya’s Amos Kipruto in what was just the Ugandan’s second race over the distance.
He has since enjoyed a remarkable 2026. After claiming his third consecutive title at the World Cross Country Championships, he broke the world half marathon record with 57:20 in Lisbon – a mark that has since been improved – and then produced another breakthrough over 26.2 miles.
At April’s London Marathon, Kiplimo finished third in 2:00:28 as Sabastian Sawe and Yomif Kejelcha became the first two men to officially break two hours for the distance. Kiplimo’s time put him third on the world all-time list and improved his own Ugandan record by almost two minutes.
It is also seven seconds faster than the Chicago course record of 2:00:35 set by the late Kelvin Kiptum in 2023.
“My preparation has given me a lot of confidence, and having raced this course before is a real advantage,” said Kiplimo.
He will renew his rivalry with Kipruto, who followed him home in Chicago last year and then finished one place behind him in London in April. The 2022 London champion clocked a PB of 2:01:39 on that occasion, making him the second-fastest man in a field that includes six sub-2:04 performers.
Milkesa Mengesha, the 2024 Berlin Marathon champion, returns to the USA after finishing 10th in Boston in April. The Ethiopian has a best of 2:03:17. His compatriot Tadese Takele retained his Tokyo Marathon title in March in 2:03:37. Kenya’s Daniel Mateiko was fourth in that race in a PB of 2:03:44 and will also line up in Chicago.
Another Ethiopian, Asrar Hiyrden, completes the group of sub-2:04 entrants. He ran 2:03:59 in Seville in February.
Several athletes just outside that group will be looking to make another step forward. USA’s Charles Hicks ran 2:04:35 to finish seventh at the Boston Marathon in April, while Suguru Osako holds the Japanese record of 2:04:55.
Hicks is part of a strong US contingent that also includes Clayton Young, who ran 2:05:41 in Boston, 2017 Chicago champion Galen Rupp and Vincent Mauri, whose 2:05:54 victory in Toledo earlier this year marked a major breakthrough.
South Africa’s Adriaan Wildschutt, Japan’s Tomoki Ota and Thailand’s Kieran Tuntivate – all of whom hold national records at other distances – are among the athletes making their marathon debuts.
While Feysa is the defending women’s champion, Kosgei has perhaps the strongest historical connection with the Chicago course.
The Kenyan won there in 2018 before returning the following year to clock 2:14:04, taking 81 seconds off Paula Radcliffe’s long-standing world record. She has not raced in Chicago since that performance.
Now 32, Kosgei has returned to some of her best form this year. She won the Tokyo Marathon in March in 2:14:29 – the second-fastest time of her career and an Asian all-comers’ record.
Feysa was third in that race in 2:17:39, having enjoyed the biggest victory of her career in Chicago five months earlier. The Ethiopian pulled away from the field to win the 2025 race in 2:14:57, more than two minutes ahead of compatriot Megertu Alemu.
Alemu returns this year, as does Sutume Kebede, whose 2:15:55 PB makes her the third-fastest woman in the field. Both raced in Tokyo earlier this year, where Kebede and Alemu finished fourth and fifth respectively.
Lokedi, meanwhile, will race in Chicago for the first time. The Kenyan has established herself as one of the world’s leading championship-style marathon racers, having won the New York Marathon in 2022 before taking back-to-back Boston titles in 2025 and 2026.
She retained her Boston crown in April in 2:18:51, with two more Chicago entrants – Loice Chemnung and Mary Ngugi-Cooper – completing the podium. Chicago will provide Lokedi with her first opportunity to race one of the flatter, faster courses on the major marathon circuit.
Brillian Kipkoech is another Kenyan arriving on the back of a victory. She improved her PB to 2:17:05 to win in Hamburg in April and is one of seven women in the field with a best inside 2:18. Degitu Azimeraw, the 2021 London runner-up, is another member of that group. Chemnung, Joan Kilimo, Magdalyne Masai, Fantu Worku and Ngugi-Cooper have all broken 2:20.
Kilimo, just 22, achieved her 2:18:40 best when finishing runner-up in Barcelona in March, while Worku ran 2:19:08 for third in Dubai at the start of February.
The home challenge includes Susanna Sullivan, Natosha Rogers, Sara Hall and Dakotah Popehn. Emma Grace Hurley, meanwhile, is among the intriguing debutantes. She returns to Chicago having set a US 8km record at the Shamrock Shuffle earlier this year, while Mexico’s Laura Galvan and Great Britain’s Amy-Eloise Neale will also contest their first marathons.

articles.title_zh: Nobel Prize in literature to be awarded in Stockholm | World News | 2news.com
articles.content_orig:
FILE - A Nobel medal is seen at the Swedish ambassador's residence in London, Dec. 8, 2020.
STOCKHOLM (AP) — The Nobel Prize in literature will be awarded Thursday by the Swedish Academy in Stockholm.
Last year, Hungarian writer László Krasznahorkai , whose surreal and anarchic novels combine a bleak world view with mordant humor, won the Nobel Prize in literature for work the judges said upholds the power of art in the midst of “apocalyptic terror.”
Three science awards were announced earlier this week. The Nobel for medicine went to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The physics award recognized a scientist’s efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos. The chemistry prize recognized two scientists for untangling mysterious mirror images in molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs.
This week ends with Friday's peace prize . The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization.
Dazio reported from Berlin.

articles.title_orig: 3 takeaways from World Dairy Expo 2026
articles.title_zh: 3 takeaways from World Dairy Expo 2026
articles.content_orig:
Forget fluid milk. Butterfat and protein drive profits as AI technology and automation become essential tools for survival.
World Dairy Expo 2026 delivered three unmistakable messages:
Butterfat and protein are hot.
Artificial intelligence is infiltrating every corner of dairy operations.
The labor crisis isn't going away.
The rolling herd average is dead. Long live components.
"I would say the rolling herd average needs to have a tombstone erected on it. We need to be thinking about pounds of components per day," said Corey Geiger, lead dairy economist at CoBank, during a session featuring a dairy nutritionist, a geneticist and a farmer.
The numbers tell the story: Cottage cheese has exploded with double-digit growth in the past year, Geiger said, becoming the No. 1 driver of dairy sales. Protein shakes and yogurt — especially Greek yogurt — follow close behind.
The market has spoken. Butterfat and protein aren't just hot; they're the future.
No humanoid milkers roamed the trade show floor, but artificial intelligence has arrived on dairy farms, and it's moving fast.
Related: Dairy Margin Coverage sign-up opens Oct. 5
Herd-i, a New Zealand company making its U.S. debut, showcased AI-powered cameras that detect lameness and score body condition the moment cows exit the parlor. The system captures video at every milking, analyzes it instantly and delivers insights to farmers' mobile devices.
Lameness scores range from 0 to 3, measured to two decimal points. Body condition scores run 1 to 5, tracking energy and physical condition in real time.
The proof? After four years in New Zealand monitoring 150,000 cows, the company claims farms have seen a 40% reduction in lameness and 41% drop in antibiotic costs.
Now, Herd-i is rolling out its product across the U.S. through a Founding Farmers Program in New York, California, Idaho, Texas and Wisconsin.
Herd-i isn't alone. FutureCow unveiled its Axis robotic teat scrubber for rotary parlors, using advanced AI cameras to nail accuracy and positioning.
The message is clear: AI isn't coming to dairy farms — it's already here.
Dairy farmers have been sounding the alarm for years: They need reliable, legal labor. Now.
During a panel discussion led by Rep. Glenn "GT" Thompson, R-Pa., chairman of the House Ag Committee, dairy farmers voiced their fears. Immigration raids are stripping farms of workers who perform the daily tasks that keep operations running.
The response? More farmers are turning to robots.
But robots aren't a simple fix. They're cheaper than before, but they still demand significant construction and farm redesign.
GEA is betting on a middle ground with its new DairyProX milking units, which it unveiled at the show. It brings robotic efficiency to conventional parlors. The units handle stimulation, teat cleaning, fore-stripping, milking and post-dipping automatically. Workers just attach the units, and that's it.
Related: Dairy farmers feeling the margin squeeze
The pitch is simple: Fewer tasks per worker means fewer workers are needed.
While it only works on "subway style" parlors for now, it's another option for an industry desperate for solutions.
You’ll see more in-depth coverage on labor and dairy components in the next few weeks. In the meantime, click on the slideshow to see highlights from the show.
Editor, American Agriculturist
Chris Torres, editor of American Agriculturist, previously worked at Lancaster Farming, where he started in 2006 as a staff writer and later became regional editor. Torres is a seven-time winner of the Keystone Press Awards , handed out by the Pennsylvania Press Association, and he is a Pennsylvania State University graduate.
Torres says he wants American Agriculturist to be farmers' "go-to product, continuing the legacy and high standard (former American Agriculturist editor) John Vogel has set." Torres succeeds Vogel, who retired after 47 years with Farm Progress and its related publications.
"The news business is a challenging job," Torres says. "It makes you think outside your small box, and you have to formulate what the reader wants to see from the overall product. It's rewarding to see a nice product in the end."
Torres' family is based in Lebanon County, Pa. His wife grew up on a small farm in Berks County, Pa., where they raised corn, soybeans, feeder cattle and more. Torres and his wife are parents to three young boys.

articles.title_orig: Russia dismisses reports of second plague case as ‘false information’
articles.title_zh: Russia dismisses reports of second plague case as ‘false information’
articles.content_orig:
What we know about Russia’s suspected plague case
Russia has dismissed media reports of a second suspected case of pneumonic plague in Siberia, as the World Health Organization (WHO) urged Moscow to formally respond to its inquiry regarding the reports.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Wednesday that “the vast majority of what the media is reporting regarding this situation is false information”, in response to a question about reports of a second case.
Peskov said that information on the suspected cases should be derived from official statements by Russia’s health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor.
Russia’s health regulator said there were no infections detected among staff after a plague institute worker died from pneumonia. The origin of the illness remains unknown, prompting international concern that the case could involve the plague.
Russia acknowledged on Sunday that a 28-year-old woman employed at a plague research institute in Siberia’s Irkutsk died after she was diagnosed with a “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”, prompting global concern over a suspected plague case.
The United States, the European Union and the WHO have all called on Russia to be transparent about the situation.
US President Donald Trump told reporters on Wednesday when asked whether it’s possible the infection was from a bioweapon, “We do not think so.”
“They are saying it is very much under control,” he said, adding “Russia is not saying much either.”
Trump confirmed he has spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin, and when asked about what US intelligence agencies are reporting, Trump said the two sides are “in very deep discussions” and that they would likely be able to provide an update “probably tomorrow.”
WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus urged Russia to clarify “media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause” at the Irkutsk institute.
“We have received information from two media outlets, one of them is Russian,” Tedros said in a briefing on Wednesday, adding, “We asked Russia to respond to that.”
“We cannot ignore any reporting that comes,” the WHO chief said.
WHO Director of Epidemic and Pandemic Management Maria Van Kerkhove said the UN agency does not know the “causative agent” behind the death in the first suspected case.
In a briefing, Van Kerkhove said, “We don’t understand how she was infected.”
“We need information in a timely way. We need regular information. We need answers to the follow-up of the questions that we have asked,” she added.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) described the risk to the United States from the suspected pneumonic plague case as “extremely low”.
CDC Director Erica Schwartz said on Wednesday that the US agency is working with the departments of Homeland Security, State, Defense and other agencies to monitor people travelling from the area.
The CDC has a health station at New York City’s John F Kennedy International Airport that can screen travellers coming from the Siberian region, she added.
About 200 people per year travel from the Siberian region to the United States, a Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson told the Reuters news agency.
Direct flights between Russia and the US have been suspended since the start of the Ukraine war in 2022.
“What we’re doing from a whole of government standpoint is we’re making sure that we understand exactly what that threat is,” Schwartz said at the Wall Street Journal’s The Future of Health event in Washington, DC.
“At this time, there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States, but CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely,” the CDC said in a separate statement.

articles.title_zh: Value Group Brings Its Integrated Global IROPS Management Model to the World Aviation Festival
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
LISBON, Portugal, October 08, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )-- Value Group , a leading provider of integrated aviation disruption management solutions , returns to the World Aviation Festival as a Gold Sponsor , reinforcing its role in the evolution of airline disruption management. From 13 to 15 October at FIL in Lisbon , the event is one of the aviation industry's leading international technology conferences and exhibitions, bringing together airlines, airports and travel technology companies worldwide.
At stand 1-180 , Value Group will showcase the evolution of its integrated disruption management model and the RUBIK digital ecosystem , demonstrating how technology, operations and governance can work together as one connected system to manage irregular operations more effectively at both global and local level.
Over the past year, the company has expanded its international footprint while further evolving its technology platform and operating model, moving from individual disruption services to a more integrated and global IROPS management model , supported by strong local execution and 24/7/365 operations. Today, Value Group works with 90+ airline and airport partners across a network of more than 430 airports and stations worldwide.
Recent operational events have demonstrated the value of this integrated approach. During the Etna eruption , Value Group assisted almost 350 flights and 60,000 passengers across four airports . The recent UK airspace disruption following the NATS system failure further highlighted the importance of combining rapid local response, centralized coordination and proactive event readiness .
" Disruptions can no longer be managed as a collection of separate problems. Technology, operations, passenger experience and cost control need to work as part of one integrated model - said Thomas Sergnese and Daniele Bocchieri, Co-CEOs of Value Group -. At the WAF, we want to show how airlines can achieve consistent global governance of IROPS while still enabling fast and effective action at local level".
At the premier aviation technology exhibition, Value Group presents the latest evolution of RUBIK , the company's technology ecosystem for disruption management. Visitors will be able to explore solutions designed to support self-handling, end-to-end management and traceability of disruption processes, and real-time visibility across operations and costs.
Economic governance is another central pillar of Value Group's model. Through its flat-rate model and hedging mechanisms , the company helps airlines achieve greater predictability and control over disruption-related costs, including during periods of exceptional demand and increased pressure on accommodation, transportation and other passenger assistance services. This extends the operational model by giving airlines greater financial visibility, control and predictability when managing IROPS.
On 13 October, Thomas Sergnese, Co-CEO & CCO of Value Group, will deliver a 15-minute presentation entitled 'Global Oversight, Local Action: Rethinking IROPS Through Technology' about how technology can provide airlines with global consistency and full traceability across disruption management processes while preserving the autonomy and effectiveness of local operations. The session will also address how a more integrated technological approach can reduce airport workload, improve operational responsiveness and deliver a smoother passenger experience during disruptions.
